speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the terms of Standing Order 43 I rise to move a motion of urgent and pressing necessity. This weekend's oil blow-out in the North Sea having underscored the immense risks of offshore drilling, and given that a similar blow-out in the Beaufort Sea could not be properly contained or cleaned up, according to reports from the Department of the Environment, because of limited technology and the inaccessibility of the drilling area, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under the provisions of Standing Order 43, I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to move a motion dealing with an urgent matter of pressing necessity.
In view of the fact that under Bill C-39 the government is delaying passage and consideration of a bill to review the Bank Act; since the chartered banks create 84 per cent of the money supply by coining the national credit thus contributing to increasing excessively the gross national debt and since the Bank Act now in effect is somewhat a monopoly of credit and thus maintains a private monetary system similar to the public monetary system, I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):
That the House urge the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) to introduce as soon as possible a bill to review the Bank Act as well as the Bank of Canada Act so as to authorize the latter to grant long-term loans to the federal and provincial governments at interest rates not exceeding normal administration costs, in order to restrict the growth of public debts.

subsubtopic: REASON FOR DELAY OF DECENNIAL REVISION OF BANK ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance.
As, according to the law, the Canadian government must present a bill to amend the Bank Act every ten years, can the minister tell the House what major reasons of public interest have been invoked to delay the introduction of such a bill? speakeroldname: Hon. Donald S. Macdonald (Minister of Finance):
subsubtopic: REASON FOR DELAY OF DECENNIAL REVISION OF BANK ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are two reasons. First, we have received many representations from a few groups, not only those interested in the white paper, but also credit unions and caisses populaires from everywhere in Canada. We are now studying the representations concerning the white paper. We have delayed introducing a bill to amend the Bank Act, in order to make decisions in the light of those representations.
There are also many technical and legal problems involved in that bill. However, 1 trust that by early summer we will have solved them and that by fall we will be in a position to present Parliament with a final text of the bill. I must say that I am willing to discuss the new measures providing for an extension of the present Bank Act, and we will surely have the opportunity of doing so in the House and in committee.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Treasury Board) moved
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
that Bill C-20, respecting the office of the Auditor General of Canada and matters related or incidental thereto, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in recent months, on several occasions 1 have spoken about the importance that my colleagues and I attach to some of the administrative practices in the federal
April 25, 1977

public service. I have had occasion to enumerate several times the various initiatives we are taking in this field. I am very happy to have another opportunity on this occasion.
You may recall the statements I made in mid-November in presenting the House with a progress report on financial administration in the public service. I said then that I trusted the report would demonstrate both the priority the government attached to improvements in financial administration and the substantial progress that had been made already. A few days later I announced that we were appointing a royal commission of inquiry on financial organization and accountability. I said that one of the basic aspects of its mandate was to ensure that our levels of management and control were the highest attainable. In these and other statements, such as when the government expenditure management course for senior executives began, I emphasized the dedication that this government has toward improving and fostering good administrative practices and procedures. Today I want to outline for the House one of the more significant pieces of legislation toward that end.
The bill before the House, Bill C-20, derives its importance from the very unique position held by the office of Auditor General of Canada in the intricate system of checks and balances which is used to ensure that public funds are handled efficiently, effectively and, most importantly, in accordance with the wishes of parliament and this House. Your Honour will recall the efforts that have been made in the past to prepare legislation to clarify the duties of the Auditor General, to broaden his mandate and to reinforce his independence. Those efforts culminated in the establishment, by the Auditor General, of an independent review committee to review and to report upon what should be the role, responsibilities and reporting procedures of that office. That committee's report was tabled in the House on April 14, 1975.
The legislation that we are now considering has been developed from that report, in very close consultation with the Auditor General and members of his staff. With the exception of some minor points that I understand may be raised at the committee stage, I am pleased to report that the Auditor General and the members of the review committee have given their unqualified endorsement to the provisions of this bill. They unanimously feel that it meets the spirit of the independent review committee's report and implements its recommendations.
This draft legislation addressed itself to two basic issues. First, the independence of the Auditor General and, second, the scope of the audit that he will be required to perform. There are several provisions in the bill which clearly show the government's determination, if approved by the House, to strengthen the independence of that office.
Clause 10, for example, would enable the Auditor General to decide whether a request from the governor in council to undertake any special assignment would interfere with his primary responsibilities. He would then have the option to accept or to refuse the assignment if he felt there was any conflict. Clause 14 would authorize the delegation to the Auditor General of the powers, the duties and the conditions
Auditor General Act
normally exercised or set by the Public Service Commission so that he would be able to establish the selection standards used in recruiting staff for his office.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Just for his?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Just for his. That clause would also authorize the Auditor General to contract for whatever professional services he considers necessary to fulfil his responsibilities. Such contracts would have to be written in accordance with the appropriate contract regulations of the government. The Auditor General would be freed from the need to seek the prior approval of Treasury Board.
Clause 15 would delegate to the Auditor General the powers, the duties and the functions of Treasury Board relating to personnel management of his own staff. In other words, Bill C-20 would establish the Auditor General as a separate employer. Clause 17 of the bill would enable the Auditor General to establish the classification levels for the staff of his office. While the Auditor General will continue to submit his estimates to Treasury Board for approval and subsequent deliberation by parliament, clause 19 of the bill would empower him to make a special report to the House in the event that amounts provided for his office in the estimates submitted to parliament are, in his opinion, inadequate to enable him to fulfil the responsibilities of his office.
In addition, this bill empowers the Auditor General at any time to make a special report to this House on any matter of importance or urgency the consideration of which he feels should not be deferred until the publication of his annual report. Finally, in order to provide the Auditor General with the maximum possible flexibility in the utilization of his annual appropriations, clause 20 of the bill exempts that office from the provisions of the Financial Administration Act requiring the division of appropriations into allotments.
I turn at this stage to the second of the basic issues that this bill addresses, which is the scope of the audit that the Auditor General would be required to perform. Clause 7 of the bill would make it mandatory for the Auditor General to report on anything observed in carrying on the work of his office that he considers to be of significant nature that should be brought to the attention of the House of Commons.
Under this new legislation the Auditor General would be expected to make observations whenever it was found that government accounts had not been faithfully or properly kept or public money had not been fully accounted for. He would still be expected to call to the attention of the House any lack of essential record or any cases where procedures were insufficient to safeguard public property or effectively to check the assessment, collection and proper allocation of public revenues. Similarly, he would still be required to report any cases where it had been found that money had been expended for purposes other than those for which it was appropriated by parliament.
These traditional duties of the Auditor General are again detailed in paragraphs (a), (b) and (c) of clause 7 of the bill. In addition, the Auditor General would henceforth be required, under clause 7, to call attention to any case in which

April 25, 1977
Auditor General Act
he has observed that money has been expended without due regard to economy or efficiency, or satisfactory procedures have not been established to measure and report the effectiveness of programs where such procedures could appropriately and reasonably be implemented.
I think it will be seen that those two paragraphs substantially broaden the mandate of the Auditor General. They have been drafted in such a way as to meet two important criteria. First, they maintain the constitutional responsibility of the government to ensure the effectiveness of its programs and the complementary responsibility of the opposition parties to evaluate their effectiveness.
Second, they meet the concern expressed by the independent review committee that the Auditor General be empowered to assess what value for money Canadian taxpayers are getting, but defining this authority to protect him from the possibility of being drawn into policy matters which are not in his domain or mandate, or into partisan political debate. It is because of this need to protect the Auditor General's office that the legislation proposes that the Auditor General shall be empowered to make observations on the economy and efficiency of public expenditures, both being concepts which can be technically defined. His powers or mandate regarding the effectiveness of expenditures, however, will be restricted to an assessment of the procedures which have been established to measure the quality of government programs. Clause 12 of the proposed legislation would clarify and broaden the Auditor General's right of access to the information which he must obtain in order to perform his duties.
I should point out that had the wording of section 57(1) of the Financial Administration Act been retained, it would have been possible, through the passage of any legislation subsequent to the adoption of Bill C-20, to restrict the Auditor General's right to access to information by the simple expedient of including the rather innocuous-sounding phrase, "notwithstanding any other act", and so on. But the introduction to clause 12 ensures that the access to information provisions of the legislation to which I have referred would prevail against all other acts unless parliament itself were to decide specifically and explicitly otherwise in subsequently approved legislation.
In order to assist the Auditor General to fulfil his responsibilities as auditor of the accounts of Canada, clause 13 of this legislation grants him new powers in respect of Crown corporations. The Financial Administration Act in its present form already states that the Auditor General is eligible to be appointed as auditor or joint auditor of Crown corporations. It is felt, however, that his access to information pertaining to Crown corporations, for which he is neither auditor nor joint auditor, should be enhanced. That is why this clause would empower him to request from a Crown corporation such information and explanation which is, in his opinion, necessary to enable him to fulfil his responsibilities as the auditor of the accounts of Canada. Moreover, if the Auditor General should

feel that the response of a Crown corporation to such a request was insufficient, he would have authority to so advise the cabinet, or the governor in council, who in turn would be empowered to direct the Crown corporation to provide that information.
I have purposely been dwelling at some length, Mr. Speaker, on details of this legislation, since the government considers the specific audit duties of the Auditor General of Canada to be of considerable importance. I hope that hon. members will carefully review the proposed legislation at the committee stage in order to ensure that the proposed extension of this officer's mandate will in no way prejudice the most thorough fulfilment of his duties to parliament.
I have already referred to changes in the Auditor General's responsibilities relative to Crown corporations. 1 think hon. members will appreciate that this is only one aspect of the complex matters involved in reviewing the direction and control of Crown corporations. A complete review of Crown corporations is under way by the government and, indeed, draft legislation will be presented in the not too distant future for the consideration of the House. This is another of the initiatives which can be added to the fairly long list I mentioned earlier, and it again demonstrates clearly the importance this government attaches to financial management and control.
This omnibus Crown corporation legislation will propose significant amendments to part VIII of the Financial Administration Act which defines the statutory requirements for financial administration and disclosure by Crown corporations. Although my primary, but by no means exclusive, interest as President of the Treasury Board in this draft legislation centres on matters related to allocations control, I am also interested in matters relating to the administration of funds by Crown corporations.
The selection of the corporate mechanism to achieve the fulfilment of national policy objectives is predicated to a great extent on the operational advantages which are enjoyed by commercial corporations, as opposed to the operating requirements imposed on government departments and agencies. The proposed legislation to which I referred would ensure, I hope, that the financial probity and rectitude which is a basic requirement in the utilization of public funds is retained without unreasonably prejudicing operational flexibility.
I know, through recent discussions of this issue, particularly in the public accounts committee, that hon. members are concerned about this problem. 1 trust, therefore, that they will be able to support the measures which will be detailed in the legislation shortly to be announced and which relate directly to the legislation we are considering. I say this because the one will enhance the other, although the executive decisions will, of course, be left to the government.
I should like to take this opportunity to express the government's intention to create the position of comptroller general of Canada.

speechtext:
Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: This is a wonderful flip-flop.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: This is being done in keeping with the principal recommendations made in the 1976 annual report of the Auditor General.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Jack is already making his weight felt.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Judging by the reaction of hon. members, there has been a great deal of speculation and confusion on this matter. Certainly, the government was both puzzled and concerned by the Auditor General's description, on several occasions, of this proposed official as being the chief financial officer or umpire of the government. The potential ramifications of that concept would have impacted on many other facets of management beyond financial administration, per se, important though that function is. Because of the complex issues that it raised and the numerous questions related to it, the government felt that a thorough review of the proposal was required before any organizational changes necessary for its implementation were made.
1 am pleased to report that after a long and detailed series of constructive discussions which 1 held personally with the Auditor General we have been able to clarify the intent of his recommendation and to reach a clear understanding of the duties, responsibilities and reporting relationships of the comptroller general. I am very much reassured to find from these discussions that there never has been any real difference between the views and opinions of the Auditor General and the government's objective to further strengthen administrative controls and to eliminate inefficiencies and waste.
At any rate, that stage of our examination is completed successfully and significantly, and to avoid any misconceptions or possible misunderstandings 1 would like to place on the record the salient duties and responsibilities that will be established for this new position of comptroller general. The comptroller general will report directly to myself as President of the Treasury Board. The office will carry the rank and status of deputy minister. In general terms, the comptroller general will be responsible to Treasury Board for the quality and integrity of the financial controls systems and administrative policies and practices in use throughout the federal public service.
The greater part of the responsibilities of this new office will comprise those which were assigned to the financial administration branch of the Treasury Board secretariat on its creation in March, 1976, which branch will now be absorbed in the new office of the comptroller general. There will be a special functional relationship between the comptroller general and the chief financial administrators of departments, agencies and corporations, thus enabling the comptroller general to provide necessary guidance while maintaining the principle of decentralized management adopted as a result of the Glassco commission's recommendations.
I must make it clear, however, that the entire responsibility for the control and direction of the resource allocation and
Auditor General Act
control processes-that is, the decisions as to which agencies and departments will be allocated resources in the first place, and how much-will not be changed and that responsibility, which is a fundamental policy responsibility, will rest with the secretary of Treasury Board.
The comptroller general's authority and responsibility will apply to expenditure control systems and related administrative practices and procedures designed to operate after and within the authorization of the allocation of resources by the government and, of course, by parliament. By this action, this appointment, which will entail a major restructuring of the Treasury Board secretariat, will reiterate our determination to maintain the highest possible standards of control through the creation of an office which could best be described as that of the chief financial administrator of the federal public service.
All these initiatives which I have listed today, the Auditor General legislation, the very important piece of legislation before us now, the impending Crown corporation legislation which will affect the Financial Administration Act, and particularly the appointment of a comptroller general, have been designed to refine and improve what the Glassco commission termed as essential safeguards for administrative integrity within the federal public service. Such new measures must be introduced periodically if we wish to ensure that our administrative processes keep pace with the ever-increasing complexities of modern government.
1 must, however, draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that although the Glassco commission acknowledged the importance of a suitable system of accountability as an essential safeguard or guarantee of integrity, it stated that the study and development of such a system was beyond its terms of reference. I feel, however, that some formal concept or philosophy of accountability must be recognized, even if it is to reconfirm the existing one, and developed within the over-all public service management system designed for current 1977 requirements.
It was for this reason that the inquiry on financial management and accountability was commissioned last year. 1 do not envy the commissioners their task, particularly having been in my present portfolio as President of Treasury Board for seven or eight months, because I realize more than ever that it will be an extremely intricate problem to outline a system of accountability that will comprehensively and successfully link together the politicial, legislative and executive processes of government.
I have no intention of further complicating that mission. I must make it clear, therefore, that I do not consider that the commissioners' work will be prejudiced in any way by the actions that 1 have announced today. I feel that I have taken every possible care to ensure that these initiatives are not incompatible with the inquiry that is under way, thus confirming the importance that I attribute to this inquiry and the commissioners' ultimate conclusions and recommendations.
In the progress report on financial administration in the public service of Canada I referred to the actions that had been taken with respect to several of the 34 recommendations

April 25, 1977
Auditor General Act
contained in the Auditor General's 1975 report. A recent comparison of those recommendations and the work that has been accomplished to date shows that substantial progress has been made in a relatively short period of time. This comparison has been developed with the assistance and co-operation of the Auditor General and also carries his opinions on the adequacy of the measures taken to date. 1 must say that while I recognize that there is a great deal more to be done, 1 am heartened by the generally favourable nature of his comments. We intend to present this comparison to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts in the near future in order that the committee may be kept fully informed of the actions that have been taken and the progress that has been achieved.
In speaking on this bill, Mr. Speaker, I have ranged over a variety of related topics. This is partly due to the way in which the facets of financial administration and control in an entity the size of the federal government are interwoven and interrelated. My principal reason for this review, however, is the undertaking that I have given members to provide them with all the information necessary for them to fully exercise their constitutional responsibilities for financial control.
Mr. Speaker, I move that Bill C-20, an act respecting the office of the Auditor General and matters related or incidental thereto, be now read a second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts for study and subsequent recommendation to this House.
I also move, Mr. Speaker, that the report of the independent review committee on the office of the Auditor General of Canada be referred by this House to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts for consideration in the review of Bill C-20.

Mr. Speaker, after listening to the minister's presentation this afternoon we can only conclude that once again we have been treated to a miraculous flip-flop by this government in the announcement of the creation of the position of comptroller general. I could call it an amazing conversion, having regard to some of the conversions that have occurred in and around this place in the last week or so.
It is encouraging to note that the minister made this announcement today in spite of the many so-called impediments referred to by himself, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and by other members of the cabinet when this recommendation first became a topic for public debate and debate by this parliament. I suppose I have to commend the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) for his ability to change his mind and also for his sales ability in convincing his cabinet colleagues as well as the bureaucratic elite who vigorously protested and fought the establishment of this particular position. It is encouraging to note that he and his colleagues have now, obviously, seen the benefits of this pro-
[Mr. Andras.)
posal. I certainly commend him for that. I suppose I could say this has come about as a result of the development of the art of salesmanship which he derived in an occupation in which he was involved prior to becoming a minister in this government.
We on this side of the House welcome the minister's announcement this afternoon. Moreover, we support the initiatives the minister has outlined. In making that gesture of support, I think I can say that we probably wonder now, more than ever, about the need for the royal commission which was announced last November, particularly when the minister and the Prime Minister have indicated so often that it would be the royal commission which would have to study the interrelationship and the complexities which would be created by the appointment of a comptroller general.
Back on November 27, as reported in the Toronto Star, the Prime Minister stated that he could not implement Mr. Mac-donnell's proposal for a comptroller general because the ramifications of such a new position would have to be studied in detail, and that it was this problem which led to the appointment of a royal commission. If we have now overcome that obstacle, that will certainly detract from at least a significant portion of the necessity of a royal commission. As reported at page 1273 of Hansard, when speaking about the appointment of a comptroller general the minister stated:
This would begin to change the accountability picture, not in straight terms of financial management and control, as significant and as desirable as those are, but it could possibly challenge the whole structure of parliamentary responsibility, ministerial responsibility to parliament and the rights of members of this House.
As reported in the Citizen of November 24, the minister said that the establishment of a comptroller general means that major constraints of a political, constitutional and technical nature must be resolved. We certainly were oversold on the reasons for not appointing a comptroller general, but today we see a complete conversion of the minister, and we on this side commend him for his action. I think we on this side have to take a certain amount of credit for this because we have vigorously supported this recommendation of the Auditor General.
I only hope that the minister will be successful in obtaining an appropriate person who has proven professional competence and ability and who has extensive experience in a senior financial executive role either in the private sector or in the public sector, because I believe the position which is being created will probably be one of the most important and most vital positions within the government of Canada. We consider the action of the minister today to be one of the first positive responses by this government to the recommendations of the Auditor General. Our major complaint is that it took so long and that the government fought vigorously to refrain from adopting this recommendation at an earlier date.
Turning to the bill before us, this party supports the principle of strengthening the role of the Auditor General. We support any measures which can serve to improve his effectiveness and we support any efforts which will be taken to ensure and enhance his independence. We feel that only by fulfilling
April 25, 1977

these criteria can the office of the Auditor General ever hope to achieve and maintain public credibility.
This legislation is supposed to strengthen the capacity of the Auditor General to identify waste, extravagance, inefficiencies and misuse of public funds, but when we examine the bill we find in it some inherent weaknesses which must be corrected if the desired objective is ever to be achieved. So we on this side of the House will be proposing amendments at committee stage in order to rectify the inequities contained in this legislation, and in so doing to make it a more effective piece of legislation which will fulfil the objectives for which it was brought forward.
More importantly, we consider it the obligation of the government to correct, without further delay, areas of inferior management and to bring about the necessary control mechanisms which will bring to an end the waste and inefficiency which successive auditors general have made known. We are taking one step here this afternoon, but evidence has been brought forward by the present Auditor General and by his predecessor, Maxwell Henderson, incidents have been numerous and repetitive, and they have become progressively blatant. One can only conclude that until today this government treated the office of the Auditor General with contempt.

speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Throughout the reign of successive ministers this government has refused to act upon the advice and recommendations of successive auditors general. In so doing, the government has contributed very little to correcting problems at their source. Those problems have resulted from the improper exercise of financial control and management. To be frank and perfectly blunt about it, if we go back a few years we will remember that this same government tried to stifle the work of the then auditor general, Maxwell Henderson, because it did not like what he said. The government did not like what he exposed and what he recommended. In spite of the constraints which were placed upon him, Mr. Henderson did a great service to the people of Canada and to this parliament.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

speechtext:
We need not only an impartial, competent and effective auditor general with broad powers and terms of reference who will report to parliament and recommend courses of action, but more importantly we need a government which values the worth of the taxpayers' dollar and considers that money to be held in trust, to be honourably administered on behalf of the people of Canada. 1 repeat that we need an effective, adequate control mechanism which will minimize the incidence of mismanagement, error, fraud, inefficiency and poor judgment on the part of the government and its officials. In connection with the development of proper procedures, the track record of the government is extremely bad. It is interesting to note the comments of an ex-bureaucrat by the name of Douglas Fullerton who, as reported in the Ottawa Citizen of December 7, 1976, said:
Auditor General Act
In the current ruckus over the adequacy of federal financial controls, one crucial point has been overlooked: The rot runs much deeper than Auditor General J. J. Macdonell suggests, or that cabinet begins to comprehend.
We have today the most inefficient, unproductive and top-heavy central government administration that Canada and most western countries have ever seen.
During the past decade there has been a steady deterioration in the quality and efficiency of management, accompanied by an explosive growth in the public service and higher levels of pay than in the private sector-all this and indexed pensions too.
How has this come about?
One important reason was the decision, following the 1962 Glassco report, to give department heads more power to run their affairs; centralized financial controls were abolished (including an earlier version of Mr. Macdonell's proposed "comptroller").
Unfortunately, during the same period public service unions came into being, with the blessings of a rather naive government. The tough negotiations which followed led to the centralizing of government bargaining in Treasury Board hands, and new grievance procedures were adopted which effectively removed from deputy ministers the right to fire ...
Has parliament lost control of the public purse, as Macdonell suggests?
You bet it has. Even if some of the causes are endemic to all large bureaucracies, Mr. Trudeau and his advisers must accept a large part of the blame for the breakdown in financial controls, and for the decline in the concern of officials about spending from the public purse.
We can only hope that the minister, in his pledge this afternoon to work restoring effective parliamentary control, will combine that pledge with the necessary action and deeds which have to accompany that pronouncement. As Mr. Fullerton pointed out in his article, the system is bad. The rot runs deeper than even the Auditor General suggested in his report. Therefore, we have a very serious state of affairs. I assure the members of this House that they will have the co-operation of our side of the House in restoring the proper kind of control, financial management and accountability to parliament, and thereby to the people of Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Since 1965 the public accounts committee has been recommending separate legislation for the Auditor General and his office. The government dealt with these recommendations, as with many others, by simply failing to act. It should be said that the provisions of the Financial Administration Act which outline the role of the Auditor General have generally withstood the test of time since its origin in the early fifties. The Liberal government, however, in the period 1968-73 felt that the Auditor General had too much independence, too much power, and hence sought to have those powers curtailed. It did so by bringing in a separate bill which would have had the effect of muzzling the Auditor General. That was in November, 1970. Because of widespread indignation and public reaction, the government decided to withdraw the bill in 1970.
While the public accounts committee in the sixties sought a separate piece of legislation, it was never intended that the Auditor General's basic duties and responsibilities be altered. Rather, it was desired to enshrine these duties into a separate piece of legislation in a manner that would enhance his

April 25, 1977
Auditor General Act
independence of the government of the day. While the government in 1970 ostensibly had this objective in mind, it seized the opportunity to water down the ability and independence of the Auditor General,
The matter of separate legislation was again considered by the public accounts committee in 1972. A drafting committee was struck and the draft of a new bill was completed in January, 1973. This was released to the Auditor General and the then president of the treasury board, but was never made public. Nor was it referred to the House or the committee for consideration. The former auditor general, Maxwell Henderson, stated in his last report that the draft bill in that form was highly satisfactory. He had no hesitation in commending it to the House and the committee. However, the draft was never released. It was not referred to parliament or to the independent review committee which was set up in October 1973, upon which this piece of legislation is based.
The independent review committee, composed of three distinguished Canadians, brought down a report containing 47 recommendations which the committee felt should be taken into consideration and included in a separate bill. The government acted on the advice of the committee, and hence we have this bill. I believe it is fair to say that many of the recommendations and proposals of the Wilson committee have been incorporated in this piece of legislation in varying degrees. However, I am of the opinion that in some cases the government's draftsmen have been overly restrictive in their choice of words in order to amply fulfil the spirit and thrust of the recommendations outlined in the Wilson report.
While it is not customary to deal with specific clauses during second reading debate, I wish to refer to a few. Those I will be referring to are fundamental and strike at the very core of this piece of legislation. They deal particularly with the appointment ot the Auditor General, the qualifications, duties, accounting standards, terms of reference, access to information, and Crown corporations. One of the fundamental questions that should be considered has to do with the appointment of the Auditor General. This legislation varies very little from previous drafts. However, the question arises as to whether the government of the day should nominate and appoint its own auditor, the auditor general, or whether parliament, representing the people and the taxpayers of the country, should appoint their watchdog or auditor because shareholders, by law, in Canada are the only people who can appoint company auditors to check on company management.
A problem exists here in that parliament is not an administrative body and does not make appointments. However, in my view, there is nothing to prevent the government of the day nominating an auditor general and then submitting his name and credentials for an affirmative vote of approval by a standing committee of parliament, such as the public accounts committee, or referring the matter to the House for an affirmative vote. I make this observation which 1 think would enhance the credibility of the auditor general as his position relates to the people and the parliament of Canada.
[Mr. Mazankowski.)

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Do you not think the incumbent has that ability?

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
By all means. I will get to that a little later. The former auditor general, Maxwell Henderson, was one of the first qualified accountants ever appointed to the position.
With reference to the opening appointment and salary provisions in Bill C-20, an important clause is omitted. The special parliamentary committee set up by the public accounts committee proposed a qualification section, strongly recommended by the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants, that the auditor general be a qualified accountant. To be specific, the recommendation is as follows:
The governor in council shall, by commission under the Great Seal, appoint a qualified auditor to be auditor general of Canada . ..
For the purposes of this act, a qualified auditor is an accountant who, at the relevant time, is a member in good standing of an institute or association of accountants incorporated by or under the authority of the legislature of a province .. .
The purpose of this requirement was to ensure that the auditor general to be appointed possess at least the basic experience and qualifications of an auditor-surely a fundamental requirement for an office of such high responsibility in the Public Service of Canada. No such requirement exists in the present legislation. The government did not propose it in Bill C-190 in 1970, and the independent review committee is completely silent on the point in its 1975 report. Maxwell Henderson was the first properly qualified and experienced professional chartered accountant to be appointed, the six predecessors appointed to the post since 1878 having all been politicians or civil servants without professional degrees, qualifications or auditing experience as such.
The Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants argued in 1970-73 that it was essential that a properly qualified and experienced professional be appointed to succeed Mr. Henderson and that such qualification should be made a statutory requirement in the new legislation. Fortunately, the government recognized this in its choice and appointment of Mr. Macdonell to succeed Mr. Henderson in 1973. Like Mr. Henderson, Mr. Macdonell came from the private sector and is as experienced an auditor as his predecessor. In the absence of any statutory requirement in the new law, there can be no guarantee that future governments will not revert to the practice of appointing persons inexperienced in professional auditing. Unless this is put into the law, the position will be seen to remain but another job to be filled by a political appointee.
Turning to the duties of the auditor general, I want to point out two serious omissions that should be considered. In clause 5, having to do with the duties of the auditor general, there is no reference to the consolidated revenue fund. Under part VII of the Financial Administration Act, the auditor general is charged with examining all transactions of the consolidated revenue fund. Clause 5 begins:
The Auditor General is the auditor of the accounts of Canada and as such-
April 25, 1977

In my view, the wording should read:
The Auditor General is the auditor of the accounts of Canada relating to the consolidated revenue fund and to public property-
That is much the same as it is in section 58 of the Financial Administration Act. This goes to the very core of his duties. This is what exists today. This is what was recognized as the requirement in 1970 in Bill C-190 and again in the 1973 draft bill.
We have to ask this question: why are these words now eliminated? I suppose one reason they are not in this legislation is that the Auditor General or the government would be able to turn over whichever duties they like to private firms. Many of the firms presently working with the Auditor General have openly expressed interest in taking audits away from the Auditor General. There are expressions of interest from Price Waterhouse, Ernst and Cooper, and Lybrand in this connection. We note, as well, that the expenses of the Auditor General for professional and special services rose from $578,000 in 1975-76 to $2,658,000 last year, and that the estimate for this year is $5,674,000. This represents an increase of
1,000	per cent in just two years. One has to wonder aloud whether or not this situation will serve to jeopardize the independence of the Auditor General, rather than strengthen it, as the minister indicated it would. Such a course of action might lighten his workload, but I suggest his independence is seriously jeopardized. This stripping away of the duties of the Auditor General must be stopped.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
The second important omission in this clause is the removal of the word "certify" in clause 5. Section 60 of the Financial Administration Act states that the Auditor General shall "examine and certify". This bill provides:
The Auditor General shall examine and shall express his opinion as to whether they present fairly information in accordance with stated accounting policies of the federal government-
The word "certify" is replaced by the word "examine". The auditor general's opinion is to be based upon the accounting policies of the federal government, rather than upon generally accepted accounting principles. In other words, the auditor general no longer has to certify that the public accounts are correct; and this being the case, his reputation as the watchdog of parliament will suffer irreparably in the eyes of the Canadian taxpayer.
What is more, I find it difficult to comprehend how the auditor general is to express his opinion as to whether the accounts present fairly information in accordance with the stated accounting policies of the federal government, when such stated accounting policies as exist today have been so roundly condemned, first by Henderson in the years 1960 to 1973 and by Macdonell ever since. The government's accounting policies, if they can be so described, have always been, and always will be, politically motivated. This is because they stem from a fundamental concept or statement still existing in the
Auditor General Act
Financial Administration Act, section 55, namely that it is the minister of finance alone who is to determine what is an asset and what is a liability of Canada.
It is inconceivable that the president, or chief executive officer of a public company, however large, would be permitted such freedom. It seems to me, therefore, that it would be better if the federal government's accounting were required to conform to generally accepted accounting principles rather than to its own internal stated accounting policies as determined by itself. In fact, the criticism of those accounting policies by both Mr. Henderson and Mr. Macdonell is the result of their having measured those policies against the generally accepted accounting principles of the private sector. It seems to me, therefore, that clause 5 is badly in need of major surgery.
With respect to the requirements to report to the House of Commons as set out in clause 7, we note the insertion of the phrase "that he considers to be of significance". In spite of what the minister said this afternoon, I wish to point out that this phrase is clearly restrictive and could be controversial if one compares it with the latitude provided under the present Act. The act as presently worded leaves discretion in the hands of the Auditor General: I refer to sections 58 and 61. In a period such as the present, when more openness and less secrecy is being demanded, such a restrictive phrase is, to say the least, ill-timed. I believe the following words, selected by the review committee are far more appropriate:
The Auditor General should call attention to anything resulting from his examination that he considers should be brought to the attention of the House of Commons.
That is the wording selected by the review committee. I emphasize the use of the word "anything". Again, in section 7(2)(d) we find difficulty in interpreting the phrase "money has been expended without due regard to the economy or efficiency". Here, again, in spite of the assurance which has been given by the minister, I am concerned about the limitation which is being placed upon the auditor general. It seems that this onus could rest upon him to the point at which his report might fail to disclose waste. The two clauses I have mentioned do not, in my view, broaden the mandate of the auditor general. On the contrary, they restrict his ability to engage in a thorough examination of the accounts. The wording clearly requires him to prove that money was spent without due regard to the economy, or efficiency.
How is he to go about doing this? No public servant will ever admit to it. Suppose, for example, the auditor general, under this clause, reported that the minister of transport had made 133 flights on government-owned Jetstars at a cost of $740,000. How could he prove that this was done "without due regard to economy or efficiency"? The minister himself has sought to justify this expense on both counts, in and out of parliament, although he does not appear to have convinced the taxpayers that he could not have saved public money by travelling more cheaply. The Auditor General could easily be put on the spot to the point at which he might not be willing to disclose such waste in his report. This particular provision

April 25, 1977
Auditor General Act
should be broadened. The language chosen by the independent review committee, which is as follows, is much to be preferred: -money has been expended other than for purposes for which it was appropriated by parliament or value for money has not been obtained for any expenditure or expenditures.
This brings us back to the question of expenditure which is non-productive, expenditure in respect to which no value was obtained. To my mind, such judgments are better left to the auditor general, rather than imposing restrictions such as are envisaged in this clause. It seems to me that the only way we can ensure that value for money is being obtained is to give the auditor general complete freedom to report all cases of nonproductive expenditure which he encounters in the course of his work.
Again, perhaps the most prominent omission is found in section 7(2), where we note the deletion of the words "consolidated revenue fund". To me, Mr. Speaker, it is essential, if the auditor general is to do his job properly, that he must be auditor of the consolidated revenue fund and must see that all public moneys are paid into the fund. The government has quite a record of circumventing the law, and particularly of channelling all funds through the consolidated revenue fund, thereby exempting itself from parliamentary scrutiny. We have witnessed other devious methods which the government has employed: for example, abuse of the $1 vote privilege. Clearly, this government has devious instincts and uses every ploy imaginable to circumvent the authority of parliament. It seems to me that if the auditor general is not to be the auditor of the consolidated revenue fund, he cannot be said to be auditing the accounts of Canada.
Elaving regard to the clause dealing with access to information, we note a very substantial change from the existing legislation which I am sure should cause some concern to the office of the auditor general. The minister's statement certainly has not allayed our fears in this connection. We feel that the clause dealing with access to information is overly restrictive. Subclause (1) of section 12 states:
Except as provided by any other act of parliament that expressly refers to this subsection, the auditor general is entitled to free access-
This is a very substantial change from the existing language now contained in section 57(1) of the present act, which states very specifically that, notwithstanding anything in the act, the auditor general is entitled to free access. Here, again, we see a rather instant change. The government did not propose any such change in its draft bill in 1970, nor were there any such proposals in the 1973 draft. It is extremely important that the auditor general have complete and unrestricted freedom of access to all files, documents and other records which, in his opinion, are essential to the fulfilment of his responsibilities. It is equally important that he have this access regardless of what any other act of the parliament of Canada states.
The provisions in this clause, on the surface at least, when compared with the provisions of the existing act appear to have the effect of restricting the right of access of the auditor

general. It would be very interesting to know what kind or type of information the government wishes to restrict, or why this restriction is in fact included. If this is to be a more open act with more broad powers, it seems to me to be advisable to stick to the existing section in the Financial Administration Act, namely, section 57(1). In my view, as I pointed out earlier, there should be no impediments to access to whatever information the auditor general deems necessary and essential in the discharge of his duties and responsibilities to parliament and, indeed, to the people of Canada.
In conclusion, I want to deal briefly with the section on Crown corporations. Clause 13 is new and deals with the auditing of Crown corporations. Given the experiences of some of our Crown corporations and, indeed, the Auditor General's latest report, one can only conclude that the Auditor General of Canada should be the sole auditor of all Crown corporations and that this should apply right across the board. In my view, this would eliminate patronage, conflict of interest, the audit would be done in conformity with the parliament of Canada, and I think the action would be applauded by the taxpayers of Canada.
The revelations which have surrounded AECL and Polysar clearly beg for tighter control and restoration of ultimate accountability to parliament. The revelations of the Auditor General in his report on financial management and control indicate that financial management and control mechanisms are weak and ineffective and in most cases grossly inadequate. Under the present Financial Administration Act, sections 66, 67 and 77, the legislation provides for the duties of the Auditor General as they apply to his work with Crown corporations. At the present time it is unclear, given the statement made by the minister this afternoon, what kind of new legislation will be proposed, but it seems to me that before we deal with this particular section we should have a better understanding of the contents of the new legislation as it relates to Crown corporations.
My colleagues will be dealing with this particular section in more detail, but we have some major concerns with respect to the private auditing of Crown corporations and sense that this bill will give greater opportunity to private accounting firms to engage in the accounting of Crown corporations and, indeed, departments and agencies of government. While such audits are brought before parliament, in many cases we have evidence, and indeed have witnessed the fact, that these firms are not prepared to disclose information to the House of Commons in the same manner as parliament's own auditor, namely, the Auditor General of Canada.
We feel very strongly about the fact that the accountability of Crown corporations to parliament, and therefore to the people of Canada, must be restored. The very existence of some of the Crown corporations should be reviewed. We think there are many which have outlived and outserved their usefulness. The method by which Crown corporations are established, the very ease with which Crown corporations can be set up, should be the subject of a general tightening up. We firmly believe that Crown corporations should be held accountable to
April 25, 1977

the respective committee within this House of Commons, probably a joint committee of the House of Commons and Senate, and that their annual reports should be automatically referred to that committee.
Whether they will be called in any given year is another matter; but the mere fact that they would be asked to submit their reports to a committee, and that they may be invited to appear before that committee would certainly serve to necessitate their engaging in proper management and control, and that we would have the opportunity to review their actions and they would have the opportunity to justify those actions.
We have said many times in this House that Air Canada, a Crown corporation, has not appeared before a parliamentary committee since 1973. Surely that is far too long for a major Crown corporation which has a very vital and profound impact on the people of Canada not to so appear, and it certainly cannot go on. I hope that when the minister talks about improving the financial management and accountability of Crown corporations he will seriously consider ways and means of improving mechanisms whereby these institutions report on a regular basis either directly to the House of Commons or to the appropriate committee.
There are a number of other items that I should like to touch on, but my time does not permit. Colleagues of mine will be outlining other areas of concern within this particular bill, particularly with regard to Crown corporations, because, as Your Honour and I know, there have been a lot of questionable actions taken and tactics employed by Crown corporations in this country. What is very troublesome, very serious and concerns most Canadians is the fact that they are associated and bear the name of Canada which has not stood us in good stead throughout the world.
We are pleased that this bill is before the House, because it does give us an opportunity to engage in debate on a very important and fundamental matter-the proper management and control of public funds. If the minister is conducive to accepting some needed surgery on this particular piece of legislation, he can expect our co-operation in seeing that it is passed.

speechtext: There is a motion by Mr. Andras, seconded by Mr. Danson, that the report of the independent review committee on the office of the Auditor General of Canada be referred by this House to the Standing Committee on Public Accounts for their consideration and review of Bill C-20.
