subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: The hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn).

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to participate in the debate this afternoon. 1 am not going to make a lengthy speech, because a bill such as this, which is so important, should be passed and implemented as quickly as possible. Certainly, it is not a perfect bill. No bills are. It is very important that we get this legislation into committee as soon as possible, and back to the House for third and final reading, and that it is proclaimed.
I had the privilege of sitting on the public accounts committee for just less than three years. I found that during those three years we ran into a lot of very frustrating circumstances and frustrating instances when we were trying desperately to go beyond the Auditor General's report in trying to find out for ourselves, as a committee, just how we could cope with his findings and recommendations. Unfortunately, there is really nothing in this bill to help the public accounts committee. That is just as important as extended powers being granted to the Auditor General. After all, he can only go so far, and we should carry it farther. When I say "it", I am referring to the annual reports. It has been a frustrating experience. I say, with a little bit of regret, that I am no longer on that committee, particularly in view of the 1976 report of the Auditor General with respect to Atomic Energy of Canada Ltd., and Polysar.
Bill C-20 is essentially a good bill. It is very interesting that the government, the minister, and the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) have finally decided to accept the advice offered them by the Auditor General late last year in the appointment of a comptroller general. I hope, in the appointing of a comptroller general, that we will not choose someone who is, in the public service sense, so inbred within the hierarchy of the public service that he will never be able to see the forest for the trees, and that he will be thinking more as a top public servant rather than as an independent adjudicator with respect to financial and management control of our various government services. Whether the choice is made within the public service or from outside the public service, the individual will bring a sense of newness to the job, as well as experience as a financial expert, an accountant and a businessman.
It would appear there is nothing in this bill to which we in this party would seriously object. This bill would, in essence, establish in a separate piece of legislation the office of Auditor General. His powers and duties are set out in Bill C-20 in a fairly straightforward manner. We know that the current

April 25, 1977
Auditor General Act
Auditor General has expressed his approval of this bill. My hope is that it will not be unduly delayed.
I am pleased to see that the bill incorporates many of the recommendations of the independent review committee on the Auditor General's office. The most important of these, to my mind, involves the redefinition of just what it is the Auditor General is to report on; a definition and expansion of the powers and duties of the Auditor General with respect to his reports to parliament, and the right, for the first time, to demand information from Crown corporations, which sometimes has been withheld from him. For the first time the Auditor General will be able to report on the cost efficiency of government spending, rather than simply the adequacy of the accounting methods used to record transactions. 1 find this extremely important in that the Auditor General will now be transformed from simply being an accountant into being an agency designed to examine the more general question of value for money.
Value for money is today a very common expression. It goes right down to the family budget. When people have to budget at the family level, they obviously expect that we in parliament will adopt the same methods, even though we have a much greater and a much larger public corporate sector to administer. There has to be accountability. I am amazed that it has taken the government so long. I am not directing my vitriol at the President of the Treasury Board, because he has only held that portfolio for a few months.
I do not know why the government has taken so long to realize what the Auditor General has realized for the last two years in both of his reports ending fiscal year 1975 and fiscal year 1976. He stated pretty bluntly that government spending was getting out of control and that something had to be done about it. I do not know why it has taken the last four months for the government to finally decide that it should have a comptroller general. The government argued vociferously against such an appointment until a commission had brought in recommendations. Where this leaves the commission, I do not know. 1 presume it will continue under its present terms of reference-a commission to inquire into government spending and financial control. I was not here when the minister began his speech and I do not know when the appointment of a comptroller general will take place. I do not know whether it will be after the report or before the report of the commission of inquiry. The sooner the better, as far as as I am concerned.
Another feature of this bill that appeals to me is that the Auditor General, under the proposed legislation, will have the right to make special reports to parliament when he thinks it appropriate, in addition to his regular annual reports. This is very important. Unfortunately, the public accounts committee always seems to investigate government mismanagement a long time after the fact, perhaps as much as 1 Vi years after the alleged incident has occurred. It is difficult to elicit information from witnesses about an incident which took place 1 'A years ago. I suggest that the Auditor General should provide more regular, albeit somewhat smaller, reports to enable this House, through the public accounts committee, to look into

instances of financial mismanagement or lack of governmental control. I applaud the government for allowing the Auditor General to bring in reports when he thinks it necessary to do
so.
When the President of the Treasury Board announced the establishment of the royal commission on financial organization and accountability, I said in the House it was nothing but a cop-out. The government was ordering another inquiry and delaying the putting in order of its finances. I am happy to note that we did not need to wait one year for the appointment of a comptroller general. His appointment, 1 suggest, is the result of pressure by opposition members as well as members on the government side, including members of the public accounts committee, who quietly said, "We had better not delay the appointment of a comptroller general, otherwise it will look like a cop-out. The public do not like the present situation." I take some small credit for this announcement, for I, too, raised the matter with the minister.
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that appropriately on that day last November when the Auditor General's report was tabled, the minister made a statement on motions in this House. It was no coincidence that the announcement of the commission's appointment was made on the day the Auditor General's report was tabled. In that report the Auditor General confirmed what we in the opposition and the public had known all along: Parliament and, indeed, the government, had lost or was close to losing effective control of the public purse. Those were Mr. Macdonell's words as contained in his report for the fiscal year ending 1976. But instead of acting, the government's reaction was to appoint a commission to study that which had already been studied time and again. I felt, when the royal commission's establishment was announced, that the government was simply buying time in which to lose complete control of the public purse.
My greatest concern about this legislation is that it deals only with the power of the Auditor General and not with federal spending controls within the bureaucracy. Financial management and control in the government will continue to be grossly inadequate unless the public accounts committee is given expanded powers to follow through on the recommendations of the Auditor General.
Clearly, the public accounts committee does not have the tools at hand to deal with matters presented to it. This was demonstrated when the public accounts committee was asked to look into the operations of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited and Polysar. The stonewalling that occurred can best be explained by referring back to what the Glassco commission found in their report of 1963. It noted as follows:
As government grows and penetrates more deeply into the life of the country, there is a steady accretion in the public servant's share of power with each increment of discretionary authority to grant or withhold benefits, to impose or waive restraints. But, there is for officials no retribution at the polls for the misuse of their derived authority. If the machinery of government is to be responsible, at ail levels to the public will, there must be workable safeguards against the irresponsibility of officials, no less than against the more remote
April 25, 1977

danger of unbridled ministerial power. Only if such safeguards exist can public distrust be allayed.
That was said in 1963, and here we are, in 1977, still facing these problems. Our problems seemed to have multiplied many times over since this government took office in 1968. Under this administration there has been virtually unbridled spending within the public service. I know that spending has been cut back in recent months. The AIB has tried to control some government spending. Considering what the Glassco commission said in 1963, all this comes a bit late. At present there are virtually no safeguards against the irresponsibility of officials of the public service. That is my view. No wonder financial controls are minimal or almost non-existent in a Crown corporation like AECL.
Imagine a treasurer being able to approve and dispatch huge cheques to foreign firms of which he has never heard, in return for services which may or may not have been rendered. As the minister knows, evidence to this effect was brought forward by witnesses appearing before the public accounts committee.
Why has the government taken so long to realize that it has been losing or has lost control over spending in certain government departments and Crown corporations? The increasing power of the bureaucracy in Ottawa has not only led to the parliament of Canada losing more control of the public purse, but to the feeling that parliament is becoming, or is already, irrelevant to most of the public.
Let me digress for a moment. Personally, I was dismayed at the way the House of Commons was depicted in a certain sketch. 1 think it showed the attendance of 21 members in the House at 5.30 last Thursday afternoon during private members' hour. Whoever sketched the House at that time in the afternoon must have been sitting in the gallery. But I note that the sketch did not include a single person in the press gallery. Those who read the page in the Toronto Star of last Saturday devoted to condemning this House because only 21 were in attendance at 5.30 p.m. on Thursday should note that at present only one member of the press is in the press gallery.
The decline from relevancy to irrelevancy has been gradual. In terms of parliamentary control over finances, the financial management and control study carried out by the auditor general's office in 1974 suggested that changes in the form of estimates over the past ten years had seriously reduced the effectiveness of parliament's control over governmental expenditures, because the reduction in the number of votes and the broadening of vote wording which had taken place was not accompanied by appropriate supporting information. I am speaking of the blue book. It is a maze. As an example, the study noted that reducing the number of votes and making the wording general gave management greater flexibility, but the loss in parliamentary control was not offset by activity information which more adequately disclosed program costs. For example, the blue book is almost beyond comprehension. Reading it is almost like reading hieroglyphics. The study also pointed out that narrative information provides insufficient indication as to what those involved in programs actually do, who benefits, or the precise results sought.
Auditor General Act
The present estimates, Mr. Speaker, clearly indicate that a significant loss of information results when standardization is carried too far. In making the changes, Treasury Board, while attempting to improve the previous presentation, appears to have given insufficient attention to financial control. Yet another feature which makes parliamentary control difficult is the fact that public accounts do not parallel the estimates structure closely enough for a real comparison on a year to year basis. The committee on public accounts, as I said before, is always studying matters after the fact.
Possibly the biggest problem parliament faces is that we in the opposition do not have enough information at our disposal to probe government policies and actions. The parliamentary system presupposes that the government of the day must justify its policies to an informed and probing opposition. It is by means of this system of continuous challenge that the public interest is to be protected. However, the government of the day has at its disposal the entire public service which provides it with expert advice, and it is not always that expert. For a number of reasons, notably the absurd secrecy of this government, the opposition does not have similar access to public service personnel and to information in their possession. This holds true for both the House of Commons and its committees.
If the public accounts committee is to be effective in dealing with financial controls, it must have more access to professional advice. The committee must be given full-time legal counsel and, as well, it must have the power to carry out investigations independent of the auditor general's office; or perhaps, to put it in another way, to go beyond the auditor general's reports. While the auditor general, under this bill, will be able to report on the cost efficiency of government spending, I think it would advisable that an agency exists to provide the committee on public accounts with an independent and expert opinion on the economy and efficiency of government expenditures.
Bill C-20 is only the beginning. While it is a progressive step toward upgrading the role of the auditor general, it cannot by itself regain for parliament control over how the taxpayers' money is spent. Unless fundamental changes are made in the functioning of committees and the House, the malaise, sense of boredom and sense of drift among members of parliament about which the government House leader spoke on March 18, will continue.
I do not want to take up much more of the time of the House, Mr. Speaker, but let me say, in relation to this bill-I am not speaking beyond the confines of the bill at second reading-that the government will be establishing the office of comptroller general and has upgraded the role of the auditor general. I think that what should go along with this in the debate is a discussion of the standing committees, specifically the committee on public accounts which is directly responsible to parliament.
So we will have a comptroller general some time this year and the auditor general's office will be upgraded and he will
4958

April 25, 1977
Auditor General Act
have more power. But what about the committee? This is the nub of the problem, although not the whole problem, in my view. When the AECL and Polysar matters were brought before the committee, an army of civil servants came to the committee. Usually there are only two or three witnesses to speak at any one time. Those civil servants should have been back in their offices working, instead of sitting on their butts in committees. That is another thing that galls me at meetings of the committee on public accounts: we are surrounded by a veritable army of staff from various departments, public servants who sit there like bumps on a log and who are never, or very seldom, asked to give testimony. Why are they there? There are 25 or 35 of them surrounding us. Why are they not back in their offices, where they belong, when you consider that a minister very seldom asks anyone lower than an assistant deputy minister or department head to speak at a committee meeting?
We have to reform that committee. I have a few suggestions to make. In the first place, I do not like the idea of witnesses sitting beside the chairman. I think the committee seating plan should be changed so that members of the committee sit in front of the committee and witnesses sit in the centre of the room. The press would be on either side. I think that is one thing that is very important to the committee, that is, the physical change. My second proposal with respect to a committee, particularly the committee on public accounts which is trying to find out where the money went and how it was spent, is that we should establish an investigatory branch attached to the committee.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Right on.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
That branch would have the ability to go beyond the Auditor General, because the Auditor General cannot fly to Switzerland and say, "I want the name of the holder of the numbered bank account". If we had investigatory, professional personnel who could dig up information for the committee-and I am not talking about trying to find a Watergate under every ministerial chair; I am just talking about questionable financial transactions of a government agency that the Auditor General sometimes brings before the committee- we could investigate the matter. At present, we are stonewalled. Every time we ask questions, we get answers in beautiful civil service jargon, answers which I consider to be non-answers; or else we are told the witness cannot remember, he does not have a memo, he recalls writing a cheque or a voucher four or five years ago, or something like that. We do not get to the nub of the question.
So we should have an investigatory branch attached to the public accounts committee so that we could go further than the Auditor General and ourselves as parliamentarians, not as civil servants, and be able to dig up the information that we need. After all, it is we on the committee of the House who are responsible to the voters and to the taxpayers, not the civil servants. I make this recommendation with the request that we use care. I do not think the committee should reach the point of controlling the House but, after all, members of the House

who are members of committees have to account to the House as committee members. I really see no danger in this kind of recommendation.
I have vented some of my personal frustrations and I have made some positive recommendations, but I have not gone into detail so far as a clause by clause scrutiny of Bill C-20 is concerned. I hope we can get on with it. I hope we will establish the office of the comptroller general as soon as possible and increase the powers of the Auditor General, but I am still left with a pessimistic feeling that somehow this is a smokescreen and that we will not really achieve what we should be achieving, that is, bringing back financial control to the House of Commons.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this second reading debate on the Auditor General's legislation.
The Auditor General has always been viewed by the public at large as a central figure in Canadian government. To Canadians, the Auditor General must ensure that public monies are spent advisedly and according to Parliament's will in order to prevent maladministration. He must also see whether the taxpayer gets his money's worth. In other words, he must see to it that the government be efficient in their expenditures. His is a highly sensitive function that must be protected from political turmoil. This the minister realized, and he deserves commendation for it.
I was especially pleased to read clause 3, which reads:
3. (1) The Governor in Council shall, by commission under the Great Seal, appoint an officer called the Auditor General of Canada to hold office during good behaviour, but the Auditor General may be removed by the Governor in Council on address of the Senate and House of Commons.
Mr. Speaker, such a statute should have been in our book many years ago. But although belatedly, we finally have it. The minister drew a lesson from the experience of recent years, where former auditors general were criticized and almost forced to resign for telling often the government too many truths. They were then extremely vulnerable.
I feel that Bill C-20, in addition to enhancing the Auditor General's functions, gives him the tools needed to discharge his responsibilities in the most efficient way possible. I still recall Mr. Henderson's repeated requests for adequate staffing and full access to the information needed for proper auditing. The auditor reported directly to the minister, and quite often this led to awkward situations. How does one give one's superior serious criticism without getting into trouble? But once he is strengthened in his position and made more independent from the government, he will be in a position to act with much more freedom and fairness.
Add to that the right to information guaranteed by clause 12 of the bill, right denied him or practically nil in the past. The bill states and I quote:
12. (1) Except as provided by any other Act of Parliament that expressly refers to this subsection, the Auditor General is entitled to free access at all convenient times to information that relates to the fulfilment of his responsibilities and he is also entitled to require and receive from members of the public
April 25, 1977

service of Canada such information, reports and explanations as he deems necessary for that purpose.
(2)	In order to carry out his duties more effectively, the Auditor General may station in any department any person employed in his office, and the department shall provide the necessary office accommodation for any person so stationed.
(3)	The Auditor General shall require every person employed in his office who is to examine the accounts of a department or of a Crown corporation pursuant to this Act to comply with any security requirements applicable to, and to take any oath of secrecy required to be taken by, persons employed in that department or Crown corporation.
As for all the guarantees provided for in the bill to ensure a more efficient Auditor General, I am certain that no member in this House will oppose such a bill, even more so when we consider clause 13 relative to Crown corporations. The minister gave the good word with regards to these corporations. It is high time that they were subject to stricter controls. In the past, these corporations submitted their report once a year to the standing House committee and that was it; their annual chore was done and they went back to their own affairs, scot-free. In future, after passing of Bill C-20, all these Crown corporations will be submitted to the scrutiny of the Auditor General.
If the Canadian population must exercise a very strict control over public spending, it must also scrutinize all Crown corporations since the taxpayer must pay the deficit of these corporations. The minister took a stand with regards to these corporations which I believe will please the Canadian population. In this instance also we have the right to know where our tax money goes.

speechtext:
The House resumed, from November 8, 1976, consideration of the motion of Mr. Haidasz:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should give consideration to the feasibility of allowing residential taxes on owner-occupied homes and rental payments of accommodation by tenants to be deductible from federal personal income tax up to a maximum allowable of $300 each year.
80012-351/2

April 25, 1977
Residential Taxes

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE RESIDENTIAL TAXES AND RENTAL PAYMENTS OF ACCOMMODATION TO BE DEDUCTIBLE FROM INCOME TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion which has been placed before the House by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) has certain attractions. However, having read it and considered it, I have come to the conclusion that there are some extreme disadvantages as well, and that on balance it is not the type of motion which I could support or which I feel this government should support. The basic proposal which the hon. member for Parkdale has placed before the House is that property taxes and rental payments be deductible from income tax up to a maximum of $300. He has put forward a number of justifications for this deduction. He notes that some 80 per cent of municipal revenue, excluding government transfers, is derived from the property tax. He states that most of this revenue is derived from residential property ownership, the ownership of which bears little relation to many of the services provided by municipalities such as education.
In reality, and contrary to the hon. member's assertion, on the average only one half of property tax revenues are derived from residential dwellings, including apartments and farms. The remaining half comes from business assessment. In addition, unless municipalities adopt direct user charges or fees for providing services such as education, the financing of the services would, of necessity, bear only an indirect relationship to the actual use of the services.
In his motion and in remarks which he has made on this motion in the past, the hon member for Parkdale has noted that property taxes bear little relation to ability to pay. He has referred to various controversies which we, as members of parliament, find ourselves being made aware of with regard to the fairness of property taxes. The traditional view of the incidence of property tax has been that the portion of the tax on rental housing and that portion levied on business property is fully passed on to renters and consumers in the form of higher rents and prices. Increasingly, however, the property tax has come to be viewed as a tax on the capital invested in business, on rental buildings and on the return from such capital.
Studies along these lines have indicated that the property tax may in fact be progressive as it falls on investors. Any part of the property tax burden that is passed on to consumers and renters is considerably less regressive if it is properly considered in relation to the average lifetime income of renters or consumers rather than in relation to their income in any one year.
The hon. member for Parkdale argued that the measure would increase the level of activity in the housing sector and would stimulate the economy. While housing starts this year are at a lower level, on an annual basis, than the 1976 figure of 273,000, there is increasing indication that housing starts in Canada this year may be almost as high as the 1976 figure.
The reductions in interest rates during the past few months will provide an important incentive for stimulating the demand for housing this year. The Assisted Home Ownership Program
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Ethier).]
and the Assisted Rental Program, which are available under the National Housing Act, are proving to be extremely popular. They are very successful in stimulating new housing starts. This is where the hon. member's motion is completely off target. The hon. member for Parkdale appears to lose sight of the social objectives which the incentive he proposes could achieve were this dollar value incentive placed in certain specific areas.
If we are going to give this $300 deduction from income tax on interest paid on mortgages for residential homes or for rental payments, the cost to the treasury would be enormous. We must ask what social objectives would be achieved by this measure at a time when we are not even able to give adequate incentives in the budget with regard to energy conservation. I was extremely disappointed by the lack of incentive in the budget with regard to encouraging energy conservation. I believe most Canadians were hoping for income tax credits for the installation of insulation in residential housing, the installation of solar or wind devices as energy-saving mechanisms in private homes and industry and for research into achieving more effective utilization of wind, wave and solar resources. In Canada, these certainly hold out hope for a major reduction in our ultimate consumption of electrical and hydrocarbon energy.
If we want to achieve useful social objectives with tax incentives, we should not merely hand homeowners or renters a bonus by allowing them a $300 deduction from their income tax each year. That kind of budgetary incentive should be used for social purposes such as encouraging better conservation measures, a need which will become increasingly evident to all in government within the next two or three years. It is unfortunate that we always appear be following, rather than leading, in so far as this type of measure is concerned. A more sophisticated metering of electricity entering homes is another possible area for tax incentives.
By offering tax incentives and by encouraging development of new metering systems by provincial hydro authorities, massive energy conservation could be achieved. As hon. members are probably aware, control meters are available which allow suppliers to price supplies of electricity based on consumption during differing load periods. Why should we not encourage the installation of such meters in private homes through the application of tax incentives? I believe they cost in the neighbourhood of $100 to $150. Imaginative collaboration between the federal government and the provinces in this area would encourage home owners to concentrate their usage of electricity during off-peak hours and save money by doing so. The potential saving is enormous. We might easily save the cost of construction of one or two major dams or nuclear stations by moving toward the installation of these meters in every home. This is one area in which the government, if it had any imagination at all, would be moving by way of tax incentives.
I believe the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Gillespie) is anxious to move along these lines. Unfortunately,
April 25, 1977

he does not seem to be getting the support of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald). I recently sent a questionnaire to my constituents asking if they thought the government had taken sufficient measures to encourage energy conservation. The response I have received so far-approximately 2,000 replies out of a total mailing of 45,000-shows that 97 per cent of those answering the questionnaire felt the government had not taken adequate measures in the area of energy conservation.
Surely, if we are talking these days about the use of tax incentives, let us apply them in areas where there is genuine social benefit to this country not only in terms of individual taxpayers but in terms of our position in the world, because within eight or ten years our balance of payments will be severely and adversely affected by the drain on our resources in connection with the importation of hydrocarbons. This is not just a matter of conservation from the point of view of the individual taxpayer; it will soon become a matter of national survival, national competitiveness in world trade markets.
I find it strange, indeed, that in the most recent budget, at a time when it was fully expected that the government of the United States would be coming forward with a number of energy conservation proposals, our government should not have seen fit to provide any incentive in the field of energy conservation.
I should like to mention another idea which has worked well in some parts of the United States and which offers an opportunity for the application of tax incentives. I refer to the use of small vans, supplied by companies to groups of employees who encounter difficulties in commuting to and from work. These vans are driven by one employee and carry from 6 to 12 employees to and from their homes and their place of work each day. This results in 10 or 12 cars being taken off the road for a large part of the year, in return for a minimal tax incentive either to the company supplying the vehicle or to individuals composing a group which does the same thing. It is suggestions of this kind that we shall have to consider if we are to use tax incentives in a way which is of benefit to everyone.
The motion before us is useful inasmuch as it allows us an opportunity to discuss the whole question of tax incentives and the way in which they should be used. However, I do not wish to support it. Indeed, I would urge the House to reject it.

speakeroldname: Mr. James A. McGrath (St. John's East):
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE RESIDENTIAL TAXES AND RENTAL PAYMENTS OF ACCOMMODATION TO BE DEDUCTIBLE FROM INCOME TAX
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) for bringing forward this motion in the first instance, as well as those who have responsibility for managing the business of the House, especially this segment of our parliamentary day, private members' hour, for allowing the motion to be brought forward once again for debate.
It is a useful vehicle for debate; but more than that, it allows us an opportunity to address ourselves to one of the most serious problems facing the country today, namely, the housing shortage. I believe the motion deserves careful consideration. At first glance I am prepared to support it. Indeed, I
Residential Taxes
would suggest the hon. member has not gone far enough when he suggests the amount which should be deductible from income tax with respect to property taxes. I should like to see $500 there; it would be much more realistic in terms of the property taxes most Canadians are called upon to pay in most municipalities across the country.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE RESIDENTIAL TAXES AND RENTAL PAYMENTS OF ACCOMMODATION TO BE DEDUCTIBLE FROM INCOME TAX
speechtext: An excellent point.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE RESIDENTIAL TAXES AND RENTAL PAYMENTS OF ACCOMMODATION TO BE DEDUCTIBLE FROM INCOME TAX
speechtext:
The government should give serious consideration to allowing some of these more useful resolutions to come to a vote. All we are asking here is that the government give consideration to the feasibility of allowing residential taxes on owner-occupied homes to be deductible.
I have serious reservations about the second part of the motion dealing with rented property. I suggest this is really confusing the issue. There are already substantial programs for rental assistance in federal-provincial housing projects, and there is considerable provision within the Income Tax Act at the present time for the write-off of certain expenses by landlords, and I suggest the advantages are often passed on to the tenants. If the House were to agree to allow this measure to be resolved by a vote today, I am sure the majority of members would support it. It would provide the government with an occasion to direct its attention to this problem, one which, I am sorry to say, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) failed to identify when he brought down his budget a short time ago.
It is interesting to look back to the last time the question of housing received the careful attention of the government. This was in 1968 when the government appointed a task force under the chairmanship of the then hon. member for Trinity, the Hon. Paul Hellyer, deputy prime minister and minister responsible for housing. The terms of reference of that task force were:
-To examine housing and urban development in Canada and to report on the ways in which the federal government, in company with other levels of government and the private sector, can help meet the housing needs of all Canadians and contribute to the development of modern, vital cities.
The subsequent resignation of the then minister responsible for housing was a graphic and dramatic exemplification of the failure of the government to act on the recommendation of that task force. Hon. members will recall that that was a major study that covered the country from coast to coast, all major cities and urban areas and some of the smaller municipalities as well.
I believe that the hon. member for Laprairie (Mr. Watson) failed to recognize the problem which obviously the hon. member for Parkdale, representing as he does a major urban constituency in Canada, is very conversant with, and that is the problem that faces the majority of Canadians today, especially young Canadians, when it comes to their ability to be able to buy a house. I refer to what the industry calls the PIT-principal, interest and taxes-which determines the amount of monthly payments. It is not always so difficult to

April 25, 1977
Residential Taxes
save up and borrow money to raise the down payment; the problem is trying to cope with the monthly payment. High interest rates, the growing increase in the rate of property taxes and the cost of housing generally, have made the monthly payment prohibitively high.
When you take into account the fact that about 280,000 families in Canada today pay more than 50 per cent of their family income for housing, that 500,000 families in Canada pay more than 35 per cent of their family income for housing, and that another 120,000 Canadians pay more than 25 per cent, this gives the House some idea of the extent of the seriousness of the problem. Further, Mr. Speaker, when two-thirds of these Canadians in need of housing cannot afford to buy or rent a home without some kind of government subsidy, in my view we face a problem of monumental proportions, a problem, I am sorry to say, to which the government has not adequately addressed itself.
I should like to identify, for the purposes of this debate, what I consider to be two of the major problems in housing today. I have already alluded briefly to the high cost of money. The hon. member for Laprarie seemed to get off on an energy tangent in his speech and for a moment I was wondering what resolution was before the House, as I am sure you were, Mr. Speaker. Obviously, he got his notes mixed up. The small portion of his speech which was relevant to the motion before the House was erroneous inasmuch as he referred to the fact that interest rates were going down. There has not been a marked decline in the cost of mortgages in this country; mortgage rates are still prohibitively high for most Canadians.
Let me cite an example, Mr. Speaker. A $40,000 mortgage, with payments spread over 25 years and a 12 per cent interest rate, carries a price tag of about $413 a month. Using the accepted rule of thumb, that accommodation should take only one-fourth of a family's income. In other words, the accepted standard is about 25 per cent. This means, of course, that that family would have to be earning about $20,000 a year to be able to carry such a house. The same mortgage, with only half that interest rate, 6 per cent, carries a monthly price tag of $256, which would require a gross income of about $12,300 a year.
Given the fact that the average mortgage rate today in Canada is around 12 per cent, I am saying that housing has become an unaffordable luxury. It has become, to quote the often used cliche, an impossible dream for many young Canadians who want to earn their own home. In more and more cases a much higher percentage of family income must be spent on buying a home.
The second major housing statistic that I think tends to distort the picture and which the hon. member for Laprairie and spokesmen for the government generally are very quick to remind us of is the figure showing that housing starts are up. If you examine the statistics, Mr. Speaker, you will find the whole system is out of whack. The government does have one program which is commendable. There is no question that the Assisted Home Ownership Program-AHOP-is one of the most progressive housing steps the government has taken. It is
(Mr. McGrath.]
a good program, one that requires more attention in that it can be established that ceilings for AHOP in major cities like Toronto and Vancouver are unrealistically low, which means that more and more people are not able to take advantage of it. This creates a very serious imbalance between particular types of accommodation.
Since the 1971 removal of the capital cost roll-over which did a great deal to erode investor confidence in the housing market, especially in rental housing-this has since been restored, but I do not think general confidence has been restored with it-construction of new rental accommodation has not kept pace with demand. I suppose there is not a major city in the country today, including the city of Ottawa, in which the vacancy rate for rental accommodation is more than 2 per cent. I think it averages about 2 per cent across the country, though in Vancouver it may be about 1 per cent or even less. People who have to start out in rental accommodation today find themselves locked into a situation in which, even though their salaries and careers progress, they are unable to move on and buy a house, as was the habit prior to the mess in which we now find ourselves.
This, sir, I may say, has not been helped by the imposition of rent controls which, far from serving the best interests of tenants, tend to restrict supply. This is another reason why, apart from the general erosion of investor confidence in the rental housing market in Canada, there has been such a low turnover and we have such a seriously low vacancy rate across the country. I do not know what the rate is for this year, but last year the vacancy rate across Canada was around 1.5 per cent.
Furthermore, while the last few years have seen a declining availability in the rental sector, we have had this tremendous increase in low income housing as represented under the AHOP program. We have had all kinds of houses built under the AHOP program. I am glad people right across the country were able to take advantage of that program. However, it is apparent, when one examines the facts and seriously analyses the statistics, that the middle level type of housing is sadly lacking. I am referring to housing within the $45,000 to $75,000 range. That is where our problem is. That is the problem this resolution addresses itself to-the problem of being able to afford the carrying charges for that middle type housing.
The time has come for the government to give serious consideration, not only to tax deductibility of property taxes, but to the route taken by the United States which has a much more healthy housing situation in terms of inflation than we have. The government should give serious consideration to allowing Canadians to write off interest payments on mortgages, or at least part of the interest payments on mortgages, which would considerably help to reduce principal, interest and tax or, in other words, the monthly carrying charges.
I hope this resolution will commend itself to the House. It is all very well to say that housing starts are up. Housing starts
April 25, 1977

are up because of the AHOP program. Let us not kid ourselves about that. As far as higher income housing is concerned there is no problem. That market is adequately satisfied. But when you get into the middle where the majority of Canadians are now, that is where we have the problem, especially in our cities. It is a problem which will not go away. The AHOP program is absolutely essential to assist lower income people in being able to afford housing. I hope the government will even extend its AHOP program to lift the ceilings in most of our cities to a more realistic level. That is only part of the problem.
We have got to look at the problem of the middle income earner. We have got to look at the problem of the reduction in the supply of adequate rental accommodation. If you examine these two points you will get some idea of the seriousness of the housing crisis, notwithstanding the favourable statistics that the government likes to parade before us every month.
If the government does not allow this resolution to come to a vote, I hope it will give serious consideration to what the hon. member has in mind by way of his resolution. I hope they will allow for an up-to-date study, considering there has not been such a study since the Hellyer task force of 1968. I believe the hon. member for Parkdale is on the right track. He has got a good resolution. I think it requires further study. I hope it commends itself to the House.

Mr. Speaker, my maiden speech to the House of Commons was on November 26, 1974. At that time I had this to say about housing:
In the constituency of Saint John-Lancaster we have a number of problems. However, we have one urgent need-more housing; especially more low-rental housing and senior citizens' housing. I fully realize, Mr. Speaker, that this problem is not unique to my constituency, and I was pleased to hear the budget proposals in relation to housing. However, due to an industrial construction boom in Saint John-Lancaster, workers are being imported from the rest of the province, the rest of Canada and from countries throughout the world. These workers come armed with lucrative expense accounts and are prepared to pay higher rents than regular citizens of Saint John-Lancaster can afford.
The influx of workmen has caused a serious housing shortage, and because many of these workers are on expense accounts, rents have escalated rapidly, putting them out of the reach of low-income families and out of sight for senior citizens. Each and every week since I was elected I have received a minimum of five supplications for housing. One senior citizens' apartment tower presently under construction received, before construction began, five applications for each unit that would become available. Because of the housing crisis I implore the cabinet generally, and the Minister of State for Urban Affairs specifically, to rush to the assistance of my people. The housing shortage is a fact. It will not go away. If, as a member of parliament, I am unable to convince my government to alleviate this problem over the next four years, I shall call upon the voters of the constituency of Saint John-Lancaster to retire me; to march to the polls and turf me out.

The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Haidasz) put forward his proposal as a method of providing relief to home owners and renters for increased cost of home ownership. As such the measure is essentially a transfer payment, and considerations of equity are thus of primary importance. Judged on this basis, even including the $300 maximum, the proposal does not appear too desirable. As background to any consideration of the equity of the measure, it should be noted that the property tax component of the Consumer Price Index has risen no faster than other prices and costs. Against this background it seems fair to say that singling out this component of the recent

inflation and subsidizing these particular costs via the tax system is not a proposal which is generally equitable. The government has, via indexing and increasing the federal tax cut, used the tax system in a much broader fashion to compensate those who are hardest hit by inflation.
In addition it appears that the hon. member is proposing that all rent be deductible up to the $300 maximum. The proposal will thus be discriminatory in favour of tenants as opposed to home owners. Equity would require that a percentage of rent, roughly equal to the property tax content of rents, be deductible. Furthermore, a simple deduction approach, as recommended by the hon. member, would not adequately recognize the income of the recipient. Some reduction in the deduction available, based on the individual's income, would appear to be essential, to ensure that the benefits are directed to those hardest hit by increases in housing costs. Actually the hon. member's approach would provide benefits to taxpayers at all income levels, but dollar benefits would rise as income rises. In order to direct best the benefits of the measure to those most in need, a credit approach appears to be more desirable. While modifications along these lines could be accomplished, any proposal of this nature, regardless of its structure, will involve further inequities.
The ultimate beneficiaries of such a general measure will not be those who receive the initial tax reduction. For example, if house prices and rents rise as a result of the deduction, a substantial portion of the benefits will accrue to developers. Therefore a measure of this sort makes little allowance for the housing needs of different persons.
It could well be argued that larger families require relatively larger dwelling units and should thus be allowed a credit or deduction for a relatively larger fraction of their property tax or rent. In addition, the inequities as between persons residing in different provinces would probably be severe. This is particularly true of New Brunswick. Former Premier Robichaud, now Senator Robichaud, brought in what was known as an equal opportunities program, under which the northern part of the province was to have available the same type of schooling available to the rest of the province, or in the south. Services in the north of New Brunswick were improved, to bring them up to the standards of services provided in the south of the province.
Inequities would occur because provincial and municipal financing arrangements vary significantly from province to province. In particular that share of services provided by provinces, and the share of municipal revenues made up by provincial grants as opposed to property taxes, vary dramatically by province. While this is not a concern to an individual province in structuring its scheme, a federal measure related to property taxes would of necessity, if there were a uniform structure across provinces, result in different benefits to different provinces and would cover a different percentage of total costs of municipal services in each province.
[Mr. Landers.)
In addition, property tax assessment systems in different provinces differ in their treatment of various types of property. This fact would result in interprovincial differences in benefits flowing to various types of housing. The interprovincial inequities resulting from these facts would be substantial.
It is in order to raise several other points, if one is to be able to judge the desirability of this proposal. First, as a result of this measure, municipalities could feel less pressure to hold property tax increases down. As a result these taxes could rise and/or provincial grants fall from the levels which would otherwise obtain. This effect would pervert the aims of the proposal and substantially increase the revenue costs. This scenario is also not the most efficient way for the federal government to transfer resources to municipalities.
Second, while property taxes are undoubtedly a cost of home ownership, they are taxes levied by municipalities and provinces in order to pay for goods and services. Responsibility for these taxes is a uniquely provincial and municipal affair. Further, a deduction along the lines suggested by the hon. member for Parkdale might be regarded by provinces and municipalities as an unwarranted intrusion into their affairs.
Since I understand others on both sides of the House are anxious to participate in this debate, I will resume my seat, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill which is before us tonight comes, I believe, with a broad

measure of bipartisan support. As far as I am aware it has the approval of the independent review committee whose report is about to be examined by the committee to which this bill will be referred. The recommendations go a long way toward resolving the difficulties in which the previous auditor general and, I believe, the present Auditor General have found themselves from time to time.
It has always been of some interest to me to note the way in which both the Public Service Service Commission, which reports independently to parliament, and previous auditors general, who have reported independently to this place, have managed to have sharp differences of opinion on the whole matter of hiring of staff. In this regard I am referring to previous years, not to the years of the incumbent Auditor General. The theory of the independent servant of parliament was put to the greatest test when one independent servant of parliament, Mr. Henderson, frequently expressed in the most unqualified terms his disapproval of the service he received from another independent agency, the Public Service Commission. That matter has been resolved. The Auditor General is now a separate employer, which is a provision of this bill.
The extension of the audit function and the attempt to develop new methods of testing roughly what the taxpayers are getting by way of value for their money spent are dynamic and evolving areas of government operations, and I know that the present Auditor General has the overwhelming confidence of members of all parties represented in this House and that he will make a contribution in this area which will be watched not only by professional accountants but also by members of this House, by members of the other place, and by the public at large.
There are one or two areas where I still have some misgivings as to where we are going and what we are going to do. As a member of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts I have been among those who have examined the operations of Polysar and Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. Those two Crown corporations have been the subject of a great deal of testimony and examination before the Public Accounts Committee. The issues which are being exposed in these Crown corporations are deep and fundamental issues which should be of the greatest concern to all Canadians.
In the case of Polysar it is quite clear that this Crown corporation-I should say government-owned corporation; I want to come back to what is a Crown corporation in a moment-did business abroad through its wholly owned subsidiaries. It engaged in the business of excessive billing of some of its customers and the crediting of certain amounts to numbered bank accounts in Switzerland. The facts surrounding these transactions raise a real question about violation of foreign exchange control regulations. They raise a very serious question about evasion of taxes or possible evasion of taxes within certain jurisdictions, and the possibility of defrauding the minority shareholders.
April 25, 1977

If the shoe were on the other foot, if a fully owned subsidiary of some other nation were to operate in Canada, do those things and be exposed, the indignation of Canadians from coast to coast would be heard in voices that would bear no misunderstanding. We would have indignation, and rightfully so. However, the question of how control is exercised, of how such practices are prohibited and how they are brought to light when they take place, is a challenge which embraces more than the audit function. The audit function is the first line of defence.
It has been said by one or two speakers on the other side that the Auditor General should be the auditor of all Crown corporations. I find that going a little far, although I have not taken a firm position on it. This would require an immense expansion of the Auditor General's staff.
Many private auditors are in a better position to service outside Canada as well as inside Canada, multinational operations. There could be good and sufficient reasons why a private auditor might be engaged for certain set jobs respecting the operation of Crown corporations. However, there has to be a relationship to the Auditor General. The relationship I think would work best would be the co-auditor relationship.
This is not an easy matter to resolve. A private auditor who discovers an irregularity in a private multinational corporation has a major problem. This is being demonstrated from day to day in our neighbour to the south. Many American corporations are coming forward and making voluntary disclosure of payments which have violated the political contribution laws of that country, payments which in one way or another were irregular. When such a situation comes to light, in my opinion there should be an obligation on a private auditor to consult immediately with the Auditor General. The Auditor General always has the ultimate weapon of reporting directly to parliament and bringing public attention to irregularities.
I want to talk about one other matter that gives me a great deal of concern, that is, what is a Crown corporation? In the definition section of this bill we see that a Crown corporation is listed according to the schedules of the Financial Administration Act, but we learn that "ain't necessarily so," as they say.
We have the example of Polymer, which later changed its name to Polysar, listed in the financial schedules. It is listed clearly in black and white. Polysar was purchased by the Canada Development Corporation. At that time it was 100 per cent owned by the Government of Canada through public funds. We then had the remarkable interpretation by the legal officers that when Canada Development Corporation bought the shares of Polysar, it ceased to be a Crown corporation.
Canada Development Corporation by law was not a Crown corporation although it was owned by the Government of Canada. Because it happened to buy the shares of something listed and described as a Crown corporation, the legal advisers said it was no longer a Crown corporation. Acting on that advice, the directors of Polysar, with Canada Development
Auditor General Act
Corporation's approval, I am shocked to say, dismissed the Auditor General as the co-auditor of the accounts on the grounds that Polysar was no longer a Crown corporation. To this day, Polysar is listed in the schedules of the Financial Administration Act.
In 1973 there was an attempt via the estimates-legislating via estimates, the one dollar items-to change Polysar and have it taken off the schedules of the Financial Administration Act. Members opposite objected and threw out the item.
We are told by people with a straight face, holding distinguished positions in the public service in this country, that Polysar today is not a Crown corporation although it is still listed in the schedules of the Financial Administration Act and although there was an attempt to have it de-listed, but that was rejected by parliament.
My question to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) is: when is a Crown corporation not a Crown corporation? When is something listed in the schedules of the Financial Administration Act no longer a Crown corporation? We have a statute which relies on the definition of being listed in the schedules of the Financial Administration Act as a criterion for deciding what is and what is not a Crown corporation. We have this precedent and I do not know how many others, stating that something, although it is listed, may no longer be a Crown corporation because of something that happened to it subsequently. I suggest this will have to be examined at the committee stage. It is a small item in the total scope of things in the bill.
I believe the bill is a good one. The expression today of the President of the Treasury Board that the government has accepted the recommendations with regard to a comptroller general has removed the last of the differences that have remained between the Auditor General and the Government of Canada in terms of what has to be done to strengthen and improve the financial accounting of records of Canada, the government's operation and, I hope, Crown corporations.
In the committee we will have an interesting examination of these clauses. I am sure that the broad bi-partisan support which has been evident so far in this debate will continue. I am pleased to support the bill at second reading.

Auditor General Act
of members of this House in their overview and watchfulness of the accounts of Canada.
I would like to compliment the government. I do not have too many compliments for them, but 1 must say I compliment them on the selection of Mr. Macdonell as the new Auditor General. He is a very thorough man. He is doing a very thorough job. He has a thorough understanding of the degree of quality that is needed in controls. With the financial management control study completed under his direction by members of the Chartered Accountants Association of Canada, we moved into a new era of hope for the taxpayers of Canada in the control of public accounts. These two measures are to the credit of the government.
The rapid growth of the federal government is now reaching upwards and over 18 per cent of the gross national product. The incentives system within our government is designed to encourage waste and extravagance, as we have seen these many years. It is a system that has its incentives completely backward to the way they should be and the way incentives are placed in the private sector. We give prestige to ministers and deputy ministers on the basis of the size of their budget and the man-years they have within their control and within their departments. We have heard many times about the growth in the size of government. Both the size and complexity of government departments have grown very rapidly.
More and more we have moved to regulate and supervise the private sector and have found insufficient personnel with accounting abilities available to control the utilization of our tax resources. One of the things that a new member has to get used to when he arrives on the scene is cash flow accounting vis-a-vis the double entry accounting to which people in the private sector are accustomed. We believe outside that people are always accountable to the tax collector, but as a member of this House I find with the cash flow accounting system very poor control on the part of administrators of the government to ensure that department heads and deputies are accountable to the people of Canada through the members of the House.
After two years on the Public Accounts Committee I have found repeatedly that there are too many people in government lacking sufficient accounting skills, and as a result we continually find ourselves outside the provisions of statutes and the regulations of the Financial Administration Act. This most unsatisfactory condition makes the strengthening of the Auditor General's powers and abilities to function absolutely essential.
Also in our work on the Public Accounts Committee we have found that the same errors in departments are being repeated year after year. Although qualifying statements were put on audits, the same questions have arisen repeatedly as if no one cared. I should like to see provision made in the legislation to strengthen the Public Accounts Committee so that the day will come when a deputy minister would never want to see a qualifying statement repeated in an Auditor General's report.

Bill C-20 is moving in the right direction, in my opinion, but a very careful reading exposes some flaws which must be corrected. In reading a bill of this nature, written by a responsible minister as smooth as the incumbent President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras), one must search for that which is not said. In the little time I have had to study the bill I have found a few items which cause me some problems.
I notice that in the bill the government has very quietly removed reference to the Consolidated Revenue Fund, which is part and parcel of the definition in sections 53 and 58 of the Financial Administration Act. I have to ask why there is no reference to the Consolidated Revenue Fund, which is omitted in clause 5? What does this mean? Are departments of government being opened up, or is auditing being contracted out to private firms? Is the Auditor General going to have a free hand in the appointment of auditors? If so, as a member of the House I should certainly like to know the rationale of that.
Another part of the bill that causes me difficulty is clause 13(3), which provides:
If, in the opinion of the Auditor General, a Crown corporation, in response to a request made under subsection (2), fails to provide any or sufficient information or explanations, he may so advise the Governor in Council, who may thereupon ...
It is generally accepted that this bill is a move in the right direction, but if we are truly concerned about the condition of the accounts of Canada, Mr. Speaker, surely to goodness the bill does not have to be qualified in that way. I do not know why the wording does not say "who will thereupon". There is no need for a "may" if the intent of the bill is to be fully meaningful to those of us responsible for its passage.
Clause 13 affords the Auditor General the right to secure any necessary information from Crown corporations which will enable him to fulfil his responsibilities as auditor of the accounts of Canada. However, in light of the current investigation of Crown corporations by the Public Accounts Committee it is mandatory that these provisions be further strengthened to assure the Auditor General the right of access to information about these corporations where he is not the auditor. The bill gives him certain powers in the acquisition of information, but it is my claim that the Auditor General must have access to the working papers of Crown corporation auditors when signing off the accounts. If he feels that there are unusual items in the audit, he should have the right to report the matter to the Parliament of Canada as the joint auditor of the Crown corporation concerned. Or if in the future we are going to have private sector audits of departments of government, in all cases this bill should declare that the Auditor General of Canada is the joint auditor of all accounts in all matters pertaining to the Consolidated Revenue Fund. As it stands, Mr. Speaker, he is either the auditor or he is not the auditor. We have a chance to correct this serious omission by insisting that this point be stated more clearly in Bill C-20.
In the case of Polysar which has just been described by the hon. member for Ottawa West, there was no qualifying opinion. It came to the Auditor General's attention that certain
April 25, 1977

unusual practices were going on in the Swiss office of Polysar, and only through his examination of the working papers was he made aware of this. He could only proceed on the basis of the information contained in the working papers of the auditor who had been appointed. Had he not been joint auditor, no one would have ever known of the behaviour of Polysar.
This is why I claim that this legislation can be strengthened and simplified by making the Auditor General joint auditor in all cases. When the boards of Crown corporations are allowed private audits only, we leave open a great weakness, for under this system there seems to be the attitude that "those donkeys in parliament need never know what we are doing and how we are playing the business game". This is just not good enough, Mr. Speaker, in this day and age.
I should like to place further emphasis on this point by reminding the House of an interoffice memo that appeared in the appendix to the Public Accounts Committee minutes No. 23 for March 15, 1977. I found this memo surprising and shocking. It is an interoffice memo from the Zurich office of the Auditors Peat, Marwick, sent by a Mr. Matthews to Mr. Kirkwood at the Toronto office. In the last sentence of the second paragraph he says:
Of course, it will not be such a sensitive matter on the Canadian scene next year when the company is no longer a Crown corporation.
This emphasizes the point made by the hon. member for Ottawa West. The games which have been played by these Crown corporations which say they are no longer Crown corporations because they have been bought by another Crown corporation are far more serious than anything I have encountered in the private sector.
Before I arrived here, I was aware in the private sector that the Polymer Corporation was trading goods off at low values to Swiss companies where the trading profits were maintained overseas so that they could accumulate an account there on a 714 per cent income tax basis, and was lending the money back on the world money market or back into its operations in Canada. I was shocked to find Crown corporations behaving in this way against the interests of the shareholders they were supposed to be serving. The people of Canada must be assured of all the safeguards necessary when examining unusual transactions relating to Crown corporations not audited by the Auditor General. The bill must also ensure that all these matters are reported to parliament. It is therefore my opinion that we must add to this bill provision for a joint audit report by the Auditor General and the private sector auditor appointed by the Crown corporation. If the government is sincere in its attempt to clear up the messes it will change "may" to "will" in clause 13 and add this joint audit provision. As the bill now reads, the Auditor General has access to Crown corporations only when he is appointed the auditor. At the present time he depends upon his professional relationships with other auditors who have been appointed to examine specific Crown corporations.
Auditor General Act
The Polysar case mentioned by the hon. member for Ottawa West is a test case illustrating where this relationship broke down. At the time their questionable behaviour was discovered the then Auditor General expressed serious differences of opinion, and in a letter under date of October 25, 1973, to Mr. Ian C. Rush, President of Polysar, he listed those differences of opinion in one particular paragraph which I think is completely pertinent. I quote here:
The second point relates to the arbitrary way in which the Polysar shareholders fired the Auditor General last May. I do not understand how this action could have been taken, not only under the Defence Production Act, still extant, but also because Polysar still remains a Crown corporation under the Financial Administration Act.
It is interesting to note that those two acts have still not been amended, though amendments have been talked about for a couple of years now. The Auditor General's only recourse was to write to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). That was the only avenue left to him to report the irregularity. We now know-a long time after the event-that the Prime Minister started the letter on one of his famous cabinet merry-go-rounds and managed to keep the matter hidden from view all these years. With these points in mind, Mr. Speaker, we must press for the inclusion in the bill before us of a guarantee that the Auditor General remain outside the authority of the governor in council. In my opinion he must have access to the House of Commons, otherwise there will be more Polysar deals where letters get on to the cabinet merry-go-round and serious matters are hidden in this type of cover-up.
This brings me to clause 7 of Bill C-20 with particular reference to subclauses (3) and (4). Subclause (3) reads:
Each annual report of the Auditor General to the House of Commons shall be submitted to the Minister of Finance on the 31st day of December in the year to which the report relates.
It goes on to say:
The Minister of Finance shall lay each such report before the House of Commons within 15 days after receipt thereof by him, or if the House is not then sitting, on any of the first 15 days next thereafter when the House is sitting.
If the Chief Electoral Officer can submit his report directly to the Speaker, why can the Auditor General not have the same relationship with parliament? What is the significance of the reference to the Minister of Finance in this clause? Crown corporations report to different ministers. If the Auditor General is responsible for the over-all reporting of their performance to the shareholders who are represented in this House, why can the Auditor General not submit his report directly to the Speaker? Why should the Minister of Finance have the report in his hands for 15 days? If there is a reason for provision of direct referral not being included in the bill, then why not change the bill or the Standing Orders? I will go one step further. Why should the Auditor General not receive direction directly from the audit committee of the House of Commons? If there were a properly structured committee, as was suggested by the hon. member for Brant, if it had a proper secretariat with appropriate investigative abilities, why should not such a committee have the strength and authority to have the Auditor General report to it directly?

April 25, 1977
Auditor General Act
One of the important aspects of the work which has been undertaken by the Public Accounts Committee in connection with the Auditor General's Report, has been the "value for money" concept. A great debate has been going on between the Auditor General and certain senior members of the Treasury Board. At page 33 of the Wilson Report an outline is given of what it is hoped to achieve. One paragraph on that page says:
Essentially, the Auditor General's task is to determine whether value has been received for the money the government has spent.
It is admitted that this is a complex problem, but the point, essentially, was whether money is expended economically and efficiently and whether the program on which it is expended was effective in meeting its objectives. Right there, Mr. Speaker, is one of the key concerns of those who sit on the Public Accounts Committee.
The report goes on to say:
There should be no discrepancy between a policy approved by parliament and the carrying out of this policy by the administration in an economic and efficient manner.
Further on it says:
The right of the Auditor General to report on this aspect of government expenditures has been challenged even in recent years. It has been suggested that the intent of the present legislation is to restrict him to reporting on regularity alone without regard to whether the money was spent economically or efficiently. This narrow interpretation seems inconsistent with our understanding of parliament's intention when it appropriates funds for a particular purpose. In making such an appropriation it surely imposes a trust on the administration not only to use the funds for the specified purposes but, as a trustee, to spend the money prudently, that is, with a view to economy and efficiency. In other words, the administration is expected to ensure that value for money will be obtained.
Nobody in this House who has been doing any kind of homework on estimates and supplementary estimates, and on the budget and in the Public Accounts Committee, can say that this condition prevails other than in the Department of National Defence which has been under such restrictions that they annually go through a zero budget. That is about the only department of government which has subjected itself to real zero budgeting techniques.
It is being said by senior officials in treasury that this point is too political for the government to adopt. Well, I am very pleased to see that the President of Treasury Board has today announced at long last the appointment of a comptroller general. This is an area which needs the overview of a group of professionals not endowed with the attitudes which seems to creep into us when we have been around here too long. It only strengthens the need for an examination of the productivity and the use of our tax resource, and I think we have begun to move in the right direction. The present system simply does not challenge the deputy ministers as to the use made of this precious resource.
Naturally, the deputy ministers fight measures which would give a performance reading. They would have to manage in the same way as those responsible to the tax collector have to manage. They have it pretty easy with an automatic 8 per cent, 10 per cent or 15 per cent add-on over last year's budget. This is an attitude that has been constant over the last ten
years of this government. There is an attitude within the mandarin level that our form of estimates is O.K., that they do not need changing, that the people in this House just do not know how to use them. Mr. Speaker, I do not agree with this.
The estimates are grouped together. We have aggregates. There is no way of getting detail of the need underneath the estimates. The form of estimates is grossed up and mistakes are covered by supplementary estimates. Why supplementary estimates? They are just an excuse for lazy budgeting in the first place. No one outside of the few gamesmen at the deputy minister level know where anything can be found in the public accounts and in the estimates. They are not an effective tool for the average parliamentarian to use.
Where is the comprehensive study on estimate formats that we were promised over a year ago in the Public Accounts Committee? Has the department or the Treasury Board done anything on this? I have seen nothing so far in the way of reform that would make the estimates a useful control document as has been called for by the Auditor General. Where is the intensive discussion with the members of parliament on this subject that was mentioned last year? One year has passed. What has been done?
I remind you that the Glassco Commission report of 1963 is finally seeing a glimmer of hope for some of its recommendations in this Bill C-20. That was 14 years ago. We need two things: first, better disclosure of use of tax resource, and second, a better basis of control for departmental spending. We need a single central control agency responsible for the form and use of estimates. I am very hopeful that the announcements of the President of the Treasury Board today are in that direction. The comptroller general is essential. What progress has been made to correct the serious deficiencies revealed by the financial management control study? We have not seen anything on that which is final. We spent a lot of time looking at that in the last year and doing in-depth studies with members of the Treasury Board staff.
I remind the House that we are in desperate need of measures that will, first, improve the form of estimates and public accounts; second, develop program and activity structures suitable for control purposes; third, integrate performance measurement systems with other financial systems; and fourth, develop a central system for reporting variances between planned and actual financial performance as is done in any well-managed and well-run corporation.
