April 25, 1977

Another thing we need around here, particularly in the area of controls, is some new faces. The old faces allowed the problem to develop. They are masters of gamesmanship.

speakeroldname: Mr. Fernand E. Leblanc (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Well, I do a good job at it. I hope you can do as well as I do.

Mr. Speaker, because of my many responsibilities as Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, it may seem somewhat surprising that I should take part in this very important debate. I am a chartered accountant and of course I am very much interested in the topic being discussed by the House. In addition, having served for seven years as chairman of the Committee on Miscellaneous Estimates where the estimates of the Auditor General are discussed, I naturally met his officials several times as well as the Auditor General himself. It must also be remembered that I was a member of the Public Accounts Committee for over 13 years, that is since I first came to the House. Consequently I feel that I know the Standing Committee on Public Accounts and know what has been going on there in the last 13 years. Unfortunately, at the present time, I am not as active a member of that committee as I should like to be, but I do follow its deliberations very closely. You may rest assured that I am as interested as ever in the matter despite the fact that I now have other responsibilities.
Auditor General Act
I have no intention of recounting the history of all the recommendations that have been presented in that time by the Standing Committee on Public Accounts, to which I contributed enthusiastically: nor shall I speak of the number of recommendations accepted by the government in that time, though the opposition claims regularly that the recommendations of the parliamentary committee have not been accepted.
However, I must take exception to those suggestions because I know for a fact that most of the committee's recommendations, when of course it was possible to implement them were accepted by the government.
I want to congratulate the Auditor General whose appointment already dates back to 1973 for the extraordinary and constant work he is doing within his department and the amendments he made to the structures since he was appointed. As soon as he was appointed, of course, he realized that there was a lack within his department. So he immediately called upon an impressive group of experts in this area who studied the problem and made most interesting reports.
When I say, Mr. Speaker, that the new Auditor General deserves congratulations, I am referring to a reporter who is certainly not a Liberal, namely Mr. Douglas Fisher. In the Executive of March, 1976, entitled A Personal Viewpoint, he said the following, Mr. Speaker, and I am, of course, only quoting the title of the article that would be too long to repeat here, because I want to avoid being accused of delaying the bill from being referred as quickly as possible to committee for further consideration. Mr. Douglas Fisher entitled his article:
Auditor General Macdonell Right man at the right time.
... and I would say at the right place!
Mr. Speaker, we are happy with that appointment. Since 1973 the new Auditor General communicated a lot with the committee that was referred to and he put forward astonishing reforms even if there had previously been an also very qualified auditor. I would not want, of course, to try to draw a parallel between the two auditors, which would certainly be unpleasant for certain people. I would also like to extend congratulations-

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext: Particularly the former chairman-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
-I would not dare name him. Congratulations to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) for producing Bill C-20 and announcing today the appointment of the comptroller general. There are those in this House who do not think that that possibility has been under consideration by the government ever since the month of February 1975 when I personally made recommendations to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) about appointing a comptroller general. There is talk here that the government reversed its position and, if my memory serves me right, the official critic this afternoon even suggested that this was a miracle.

April 25, 1977
Auditor General Act
Not at all, Mr. Speaker, because as early as February 75, before the presentation of the first Auditor General's report concerning the appointment of a comptroller general, I had prepared for the Prime Minister and several ministers a memorandum on that possibility and the whole thing had been discussed since the beginning of 75.
Following that memorandum, I had discussions with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Chretien) and the Auditor General and I am pleased to see that following those discussions there has been an agreement concerning the appointment of such a comptroller general which as you know, Mr. Speaker, exists in private enterprise. Of course, private enterprise can often give to the government examples of sound and good administration. In my memorandum I referred to the fact that private enterprise had created such a position and that it was of the utmost importance to avoid the waste that often happens in an enterprise, and particularly in one like ours which is the enterprise of the federal government with a budget exceeding $40 billion. Obviously, we frequently refer to the Glassco report but let us not forget that when that Royal commission produced a report of the utmost importance, amounts of about seven or eight billion were at stake and that, consequently, the recommendations made then might be a little less valid now as the budget has considerably increased since that time.
This afternoon some members referred to amendments. I hope that the amendments to Bill C-20 will be considered seriously, as the Auditor General already gave his support to Bill C-20 as it has been tabled today. And I think it is important that members of the opposition wishing to amend the bill also consult the Auditor General who is, I am sure, at their disposal, to make sure of the relevancy of the amendments they wish to suggest.
It is very difficult, Mr. Speaker, not to act in a partisan way on any committee, whether it be the Public Accounts Committee or the Committee on External Affairs and National Defence, because I do not know one member, either of the opposition or of the government, who is able to express objective views. When we express our views, they certainly stem from other than objective reasons, because we must all, of course, meet the needs and demands of our electors and we must also be loyal to the party we represent, and in my opinion, there is nothing in the House or in the committees, that is perfectly non partisan.
And at the present time, I think we can see unfortunately this partisanship take effect in some cases, not everywhere but still in some cases. When we deal, Mr. Speaker, with the royal commission which was set up and to which hon. members opposite have objected, I think we must refer to what the Auditor General himself said when this Royal commission was established: he said that the terms of reference of this commission were self-evident. The Auditor General was then and is still very interested in this commission which is not a duplication in this case but which will consider some of the existing

control problems in government expenditures and which will have to report of course in the near future.
I said, Mr. Speaker, that as early as February 1975, I had submitted a memorandum to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) as well as to several ministers on the possible establishment of the position of comptroller general and, of course, I consider myself as the parliamentary sponsor of this happy initiative from the government. In fact, before the 1976 report of the Auditor General, in which he makes this recommendation, to my knowledge no opposition member ever recommended this appointment and such recommendation was never included in the numerous previous reports of the Public Accounts Committee. It is after the publication of the Auditor General's report that the opposition has considered it a very worthwhile proposal which should be followed up by the government. That has actually been done since then. We must now pay tribute to the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras). Of course, the cabinet has agreed to the appointment of this comptroller general.
I mentioned in this regard that I have had very interesting discussions on this proposal with both the Auditor General and the Deputy Auditor General, Mr. Rheal Chatelin, since 1973, and that I also had very lively and interesting meetings with trade and industry representatives, businessmen, professionals and others who had already some experience of a comptroller general. According to them, in view of the increase in federal government estimates, it was timely to provide for such a position and above all to ensure that the incumbent had adequate powers to fulfill his duty efficiently.
Of course, the comptroller general must check into useless expenditures, occasional Financial mistakes by some of our senior officials, lavishness and, in short, the waste of our administrative bureaucracy. Certainly the role of the Treasury Board is to control the preparation of the estimates and, to some extent, the way public funds are spent.
In my view current controls are inadequate, even if we add the control exercised by the Auditor General, and a new position is an absolute necessity if we are to ensure that Canadians are well served by the federal government, that their money is wisely spent. Because they ultimately pay the bill.
I even suggested, and I hope the present members of the Standing Committee on Public Accounts will agree, that the committee's name should be changed. That name suggests that we are scrutinizing public accounts, whereas we discuss perhaps 95 per cent of the time recommendations and remarks by the Auditor General. Therefore, my recommendation in the brief was that we might change the committee's name to that of committee for expenditures control, which would be much more appropriate in my view.
I also feel that certain statements made by the Auditor General in his report of May 1976 concerning co-operation between the federal government, the current government and his own office should be put on record. He said: I am convinced that my concerns over the weaknesses and shortcomings in the financial control are shared by the government and its
April 25, 1977

senior officials. Those are not my words, but the Auditor General's. Ele also had this to say: Since I was appointed Auditor General of Canada in July 1973, the government quickly and positively responded to my requests for additional professional resources in my staff; such requests are fully justified by the situation I have just indicated, and the response obviously proves the government's concern over the problem and the serious support my office is receiving from them.
I also heard the same remarks by his predecessor. When I put the following question, before the Standing Committee on Public Accounts: Mr. Auditor General, did the government ever refuse funds to increase your staff and your efficiency? The answer was: No, the government never refused such funds. This applies not only to the present Auditor General but to his predecessor.
The Auditor General also said: Treasury Board never refused, changed or reduced my requests for additional resources at the top management or professional levels, nor the funds needed to improve professional standards or to undertake special study such as the financial management and control study or other studies mentioned in my report. He also mentioned, in his report for 1976:
Furthermore, I have every reason to believe that most of the key recommendations of the independent review committee which were referred to earlier will probably be integrated in a new piece of legislation on the Auditor General of Canada. These measures as a whole lead me to believe firmly that in 1978, when it has a hundred years of existence, the Auditor General's office will be in a better position than ever to perform efficiently as the watchdog of Parliament.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I do not think I should dwell endlessly on the subject but I do want to mention once again that I played a direct part in the fact that we are now on the verge of appointing a comptroller general, and one can be assured that I am honoured and that I feel I made an important contribution to the Canadian people, were it only the appointment of a comptroller general who will surely be in a position to control expenditures beforehand, before the Auditor General can examine them. Thus, the money of the Canadian people will be well spent and I think that they will recognize that the comptroller general has been appointed indeed by a Liberal government for the greatest benefit of the population as a whole.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member who just spoke said that it is this Liberal government which is appointing a comptroller general. I agree with that, and I am sure a great many hon. members agree that we have to appoint a comptroller general because of this same government.
We now have one of the worst economic situations with which we have ever had to deal. An article in the April 7 Ottawa Journal said the following:
Auditor General Act
The severe slowdown in the economy will affect all regions in Canada with the recent budget doing little to improve the bleak outlook, according to the latest findings of the Conference Board of Canada.
Despite the differing industrial structures of the 10 provinces, all are expected to experience 'diminished economic growth,' the board reported Wednesday.
Total output in Canada is forecast by the board to increase by only three per cent in real terms this year, compared with 4Vi per cent in 1976.
'While this forecast was completed prior to the presentation of the recent federal budget, an analysis of the measures contained therein suggests no major revisions to the outlook for the current year'...
I read that to bring to the attention of the House the reason the financial operations of this government have to be controlled. When we compare our budgetary deficit of $7.2 billion with the over-all budget of some 15 years ago, we realize that there is no way Canada can continue on this road.
I realize, as the hon. member just stated, that the Auditor General is granted certain funds in order to establish a proper facility to audit the financial operations of the federal government. Nevertheless, I think we have to exercise a great deal of care and not throw the baby out with the bath water, thereby losing as much through auditing services as we are saving because of proper auditing.
The Auditor General will have to consider the cost of auditing and the cost of contracts he undertakes with auditing firms. Ultimately he will have to be given authority to investigate the auditing of any Crown corporation, if Canadian taxpayers are to be treated justly. Mr. Macdonell will have to consider these matters seriously in the weeks, months, and years which lie ahead. I am satisfied that these are some of the matters with which future governments will have to come to grips.
We have just experienced a serious situation with regard to Crown corporations such as AECL, Polymer, Polysar and others. We should use these as examples so that we will know what we should do and what we should not do.
We all realize that the duties and responsibilities of the Auditor General are serious, important, and onerous. His task would be much easier to carry out if there were sensible considerations made and a limit in the minds of those who do the actual spending of public funds. This would have to start with the government itself and be followed through by deputy ministers and other senior public servants. Unless those who approve purchases, projects, studies and contracts have their minds on the amounts which should be allocated, there will be waste through purchasing or hiring what is not really needed, and by lax administration once certain measures are approved.
It is all very well for the government to change deputy ministers and cabinet ministers who get into trouble or whose performance is doubtful, but that does not remove waste, mismanagement, and carelessness. Those shortcomings are merely shifted to other individuals or agencies. In the meantime, is any thought being given to Canadian taxpayers, who seem to come last? They pay for all government operations and spending, and they are at the mercy of our entire system of squandering tax dollars and manoeuvring through bookkeeping.

April 25, 1977
Auditor General Act
The Auditor General recommended the appointment of a financial officer to be responsible for spending within each department, corporation, or other government agency. Actually, the existing staff should have someone who checks all expenditures, whether or not that person has the position of financial officer.
The appointment of a comptroller general is a step in the right direction, but I trust that this will not mean the setting up of another expensive, unnecessary bureaucracy. The comptroller general will require a staff, but he should be able to use the services of deputy ministers, assistant deputy ministers or branch heads. If these senior employees do not now take spending seriously, I feel sure that the comptroller general could draw up guidelines, with the co-operation of deputy ministers, which would assist him in his great responsibility and in his effort to eliminate waste and unnecessary spending.
The Auditor General should not be hindered or hampered in performing the audit of federal books. His authority should be strengthened to meet the need, and only he knows where his work runs into stumbling blocks.
I have questioned the advisability of the Auditor General becoming too cosy with any government department or agency. If the Auditor General were to give warning or draw carelessness or weakness to the attention of those in charge, they would have time to clean up their act and then slip back and follow again the same pattern of careless spending or lax management. On the other hand, if senior personnel were aware of the fact that their activities were being carefully and diligently scrutinized and monitored right within their offices, they would certainly be more careful of what they spend, of what they receive in return, and whether tax dollars are used wisely.
Everyone knows the trouble the Public Accounts Committee has experienced. Earlier I mentioned Polymer, Polysar, and Atomic Energy of Canada Limited. If the Auditor General had had the authority he needed to carry out his job, this kind of situation would not have arisen. The answer is not to remove his services from a Crown corporation which is mishandling funds. The answer is to allow him to get to the root of the trouble instead of waiting months and years for it to surface. I believe that the Auditor General has the right and the responsibility on behalf of the taxpayers of Canada to examine the auditing of every Crown corporation in Canada. Tax dollars continue to be squandered. There should not be any loophole whereby money can be spent inside or outside Canada without the Auditor General being furnished with the details. How can he carry out his job as auditor otherwise? No auditor can check books if there is not an accounting of what was purchased or where the money went. An individual could not manage personal finances for long if he or she did not know where the funds were going, how much, when, what was received in return, was it worthwhile or was it waste.
Just because the government has a bottomless pit whereby taxpayers are assessed more to meet an uncontrolled appetite

for more dollars does not mean that government employees should be on a never-ending shopping tour or spending spree. There must be a limit, there must be a value and a need taken into thought prior to that financial action. It is too late once the money has been wasted or spent without explanation or reason.
If the heads of departments, government corporations or agencies do not take seriously the spending of money of others, they should be removed. By the same token, any employee who is not performing to the maximum is a waste of public funds, whether he is at the top or at the bottom of the pay scale. I include in this Crown corporations because so many of them operate at a deficit.
A grand title and a senior position do not necessarily mean best performance and maximum output. Are these people worth the amount paid for their services? The Auditor General cannot check on that type of waste, but the immediate senior can and should, or that employee is not in the right job.
The Prairie Farm Assistance Act is an example of inadequate performance. The Auditor General inspected the books, yet he did not have any way of knowing that improper financial activities were taking place within that administration. A mechanism should be set up whereby there would be a means of establishing not only a measurement of man-hour output but of personal performance. In other words, what are employees doing, is it necessary, and is it of benefit to Canadians whose money is being spent? This bill does not seem to provide for correction of that type of abuse of labour and funds, which cannot be detected unless a person happens to stumble on it, and then no one knows how many similar incidents are missed. This is a soft spot within government financial management.
Everyone has an opinion of the worth or uselessness of royal commissions, better known as stopgaps during times of difficulties. The present royal commission will be working for two or three years and no doubt will come up with many recommendations, which cannot be of benefit unless implemented. Prior to that report, the Auditor General must get on with his job. If this bill is to be of any value at all, it must include provisions to enable the Auditor General to audit and consider every aspect of government spending; amounts, worthiness, necessity, possible duplication, mismanagement, laxity in administration, over-hiring, incompetent hiring, inefficient performance, daily output for man-hours, and many other related facts.
Control is a small word with a big meaning. If the Auditor General is not permitted to get right at the root of the causes of wastage and mishandling of dollars, he certainly cannot advise on control. As long as the government operates as it is now, which apparently is out of control as far as spending is concerned, it will take more than wage and price controls to control expenditures. To assign a man a vital task without giving him the tools to do the job is perhaps a bigger waste of time and money than the accounts he is checking.
Parliament should have more say in where taxpayer dollars are going, and the Auditor General should have sufficient
April 25, 1977

power to audit government books so he can do so without being hampered or frustrated.
I would feel more comfortable if the Auditor General were allowed to report directly to parliament or to the Speaker of this House rather than to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) or any minister. Immediately his report is presented it could then be studied in committee. The 15 day allowance before the report is tabled is not necessary.
What are the measures the government suggested this afternoon that will rectify these problems that have been so well spelled out by the Auditor General? I quote from the minister's statement: "Mr. Speaker, this draft legislation addresses two basic issues; first, the independence of the office of Auditor General of Canada, and second, the scope of the audit that he will be required to perform."
These are only two of the measures among many which the government must undertake. Only an increased scope plus the resource to ensure that the Auditor General has adequate staff will suffice. The minister made a gesture under Clause 19 of the bill. I quote from page four of the notes for his speech: "While the Auditor General will continue to submit his estimates to the Treasury Board for approval, Section 19 of the bill would empower him to make a special report to the House of Commons 'in the event that amounts provided for his office in the estimates submitted to parliament are, in his opinion, inadequate to enable him to fulfil the responsibilities of his office'."
In reality, however, it requires a money vote to be passed by this House to bring that objective to fruition. This may not be a bad idea to control public expenditure, and I am all in favour of that, if it is not done with the explicit design to control the Auditor General. In view of this, the Auditor General does not have unlimited resources and it is wrong to state otherwise.
I would have been much happier if the cost of financing the royal commission, that is, the inquiry on financial management and accountability, which the government appointed just a few months ago, had been channelled into a fund to be used at the direction of the Auditor General. That department could make better use of those funds.
We have now seen two annual reports of the Auditor General, 1975 and 1976, where the financial management and control of departments, agencies and Crown corporations have been evaluated and found wanting. The Auditor General has diagnosed the illness and prescribed a remedy in the form of a recommendation to the government to restore the health of these departments and agencies.
One of those recommendations was the appointment of a comptroller general, which goes a long way toward developing and establishing sound financial practices and policies throughout government. We do not require nor is there any need for another commission to tell the comptroller general how to do his job.
I quote further from the minister's statement of this afternoon: "I feel, however, that some formal concept or philosophy of accountability must be recognized and developed within the
Auditor General Act
over-all public service management system. It was for this reason that the inquiry on financial management and accountability was commissioned last year."
As I said earlier, we really do not need another royal commission to dabble with the pleasantries and niceties of concepts and philosophies of accountability. We need the practical recommendations of the Auditor General to be applied in order to acquire sound financial management through government departments and Crown corporations.
Speaking about accountability, the first place to look is right here on the floor of the House of Commons, not in the volumes of a Royal Commission Report which will be allowed to gather dust over the years and whose only purpose will be to distract attention from the problem.
Ever since the abolition of the post of Comptroller of the Treasury in 1969 there has been a significant increase in government spending by departments, and a weakening of financial controls within government. No doubt this is why Canada's spending record in per capita terms is so much worse than that of any other country in the western world. Instead of having a strong, unified system of cash management, financial accounting and pre-audit exercised religiously by the Comptroller of the Treasury, government departments developed their own accounting and financial systems designed to suit their own circumstances in the absence of any central direction or guidance from Treasury Board. It was not until departmental spending increased out of all proportion that Treasury Board became embarrassed by publication of the major conclusions of the Auditor General in his reports of 1975 and 1976. Only then did we see any action.
I should like to put on record the statements made by the Auditor General in those reports because they underline the point I have been trying to make:
The study leads to one clear conclusion: the present state of the financial management and control system of departments and agencies of the Government of Canada is significantly below acceptable standards of quality and effectiveness.
That appears on page four, chapter 2.5 of the Report of the Auditor General for 1975. Further, on page nine of the Auditor General's Report of 1976, in paragraph 2.3, we find the following:
Based on the study of the systems of departments, agencies and Crown corporations audited by the Auditor General, financial management and control in the Government of Canada is grossly inadequate. Furthermore, it is likely to remain so until the government takes strong, appropriate and effective measures to rectify this critically serious situation.
The recommendation to appoint a comptroller general will, I hope, help clear up the mess in which we are floundering. It behooves every member of parliament to rally behind the Auditor General and to ensure that future reports by him or his successors do not repeat such criticism as has been necessary in the last two years. Canada is a strong country, but it is not strong enough to withstand the results of a continued lack of financial control such as we have witnessed in the last seven or eight years.

April 25, 1977
Auditor General Act
[ Translation]

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OFFICE OF AUDITOR GENERAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while reading Bill C-20, I was reminded of the succession of former auditors general, because I became a member of parliament in 1957, at the time of the formidable Mr. Watson Sellar. In 1960 or 1961, I do not remember exactly, we had Mr. Max Henderson, and then, in recent years, Mr. Macdonell.
The Auditor General has always been the protector of public interest in auditing the accounts of the government of Canada. I recall that during my first years in this House, I served on the Committee on Public Accounts for several years. At that time, the reports were different, so that peccadillos and minor and major faults in the administration were very similar to those of today. In fact, we must recognize that the administration of the government of Canada is in the hands of human beings, and, whether they are ministers, administrators, deputy ministers, public servants, there is always the possibility of making mistakes. Then, there are certainly some who serve their own personal interests, as we have seen, one way or the other. After all, in the fifties, we had to have the Glassco Commission to study the whole structure of the government. I also remember that there were commissions and subcommissions of the Glassco Commission. Certain recommendations were perhaps somewhat distant from the administration and far from practical. Naturally, after further consideration, certain changes were made in these recommendations and most of them were implemented.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to traverse all the ground my hon. friends and members across the Chamber have travelled this evening in consideration of this bill. A great deal has been said with reference to Crown corporations which are subject to some sort of indefinite and unsatisfactory examination by the Auditor General. By their very nature, it must be difficult for Crown corporations of a certain kind-I have in mind the CNR, for example-to fit into the Auditor General's picture. His staff, the structure of his organization, are more fitted to look into the accounts of the public administration sector, the various government departments and so on.
Knowing the number of Crown corporations and the several categories of them which exist, I would think that parliament itself exercises not one iota of control over them. In fact the government does not have any control over them either. Control means that an organization such as a Crown corporation must come under public scrutiny. That is the essence of control. One could envisage the best possible administrators working under a blanket of total silence. No control is imposed upon them.
As for the reports which are presented by the Crown corporations, and which are dutifully tabled by ministers each year according to the law, rarely if ever do they receive any examination from one of our committees. Such are the strictures imposed upon our standing committees that they cannot consider an annual report unless it is the subject of a specific reference from the House.

Going back into history I can recall when the annual report of the Canadian National Railways would occasion a six to eight day debate in this House. But to start with, the debate was a wrangle on the part regretfully of most members who had a lamentable ignorance of what they were talking about. They adopted an adversary attitude with the management of the CNR. The same thing applied in Mr. McGregor's day when he was president of Air Canada. I found it ludicrous that that was the case.
I join with my colleague from Vegreville. He and I have spoken about this in the past. There has to be a much more responsible means of enquiring into the operations of Crown corporations. Why is the government trying to hide them under a patently artificial screen, as it does by putting Polysar under the Canada Development Corporation? Even putting it under the name of that corporation is a play on words. Since when does Polysar have to be developed? Polysar is a Crown corporation regardless of what anybody says.
The legislation referred to by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Andras) this afternoon must clearly spell out that any corporation owned directly or indirectly by the Government of Canada shall be subject to scrutiny. That should be so whether the audit is done by the Auditor General or in conjunction with the Auditor General. Better still, the reports of each and every Crown corporation in the four categories listed in the Financial Administration Act should stand referred on tabling, without further debate, to a joint committee of this House and the Senate.
In our statutory instruments we have had cases where documents and orders in council representing delegated legislation had for years and years carried on, affecting the rights of citizens, without one iota of check being made as to their legality. No scrutiny was made as to whether they were within the competence of the administration, whether they were authorized by the act, or whether they traduced the rights of citizens. Now delegated legislation is subject to scrutiny. It is not perfect yet; there is some dispute between those who desire a veil of silence on the part of administrative personnel and those who seek to put control back on through public scrutiny.
It must be an accepted fact, Mr. Speaker, that since 1964 and 1965 the House of Commons and the other place have lost financial control over the government. It used to be that through interim supply and the system of granting government credits, this House could withhold supply, and that was the ultimate sanction on the government. That has now gone and I do not think there is any way of retrieving it unless one were to work a major revolution in this whole system.
It may be that with up-to-date computerized operations it is impossible to impose financial control by withholding interim supply, as was the case. But if parliament has lost control over the administration through the abandonment or gradual usurpation of financial controls, then I say to this House that parliament must insist on maintaining control by openness, by examination, by supervision, by scrutiny. Otherwise all will become lost.
April 25, 1977

I have before me a copy of the 1951 Financial Administration Act which appears at the back, as an appendix, of the one and only fourth edition of Beauchesne. As an aside, Mr. Speaker, may I say that this has almost become a collector's item. It is so out of date with so much of our proceedings in the House that it has become a dangerous book. So far as the Financial Administration Act is concerned, Bill C-20 makes reference to Crown corporations as described in section 66(1). If one goes to the Financial Administration Act which is appended to Beauchesne's fourth edition, the section becomes section 76(1) and the language is not the same.
One rather intriguing point comes up in this bill. At the very beginning of Bill C-20 reference is made, just before the duties of the Auditor General, to the salary that he shall be paid. The old act in 1951 said that the Auditor General would be paid a salary of $15,000. In 1954 that was raised to $20,000. Unfortunately, even following 1954 one had to bring in an amendment to the legislation to increase the salary of the Auditor General, and that was a most difficult thing to do.
Under the new legislation the Auditor General is to be paid a salary equal to that of the Chief Justice of the Federal Court; they walk in locked step. But there is a strange anomaly; the Auditor General must retire at the age of 65. There is no option open to the Crown to grant an extension; the Auditor General must retire at the age of 65. The Chief Justice of the Federal Court is to retire at 70. I thought it was rather strange to have the two march along in locked step so far as their salaries are concerned, but that the Auditor General, whose position is presumably somewhere in the pecking order of senior administrators connected with the Government of Canada, must get off the trolley at the age of 65 whereas his counterpart, the Chief Justice of the Federal Court, may continue on to 70, and then may become a Supernumerary judge. I have always wondered why it was necessary that the Auditor General would have to retire at 65. Then I looked back at the 1951 act. I think somebody in committees should go to work on this particular item and see why the Auditor General has to retire at the age of 65. That is mandatory in the end. I do not see why. Certainly Watson Sellars and Max Henderson after 65 had got more left up in the top storey and more energy. Those men had great energy and were quite well able to carry on. I do not mean any disrespect in saying that. It seems to me that there is an anachronism in this particular bill.
I was just wondering what role the government was proposing for the ever-expanding program that the Auditor General has faced over a number of years, namely, that Canada, from time to time, has to provide the auditor of some international agency to which Canada has contributed. Some years this can prove to be a very onerous burden because it so happens it is Canada's turn to take on a number of major agencies. It means the auditors must go abroad and are often away some considerable time. This is quite prestigious in so far as Canada is concerned. I suppose one might say all right, it is one of those things we take as it comes along. It is a responsibility for
Auditor General Act
the Auditor General. He has to provide the staff for it. It is reflected in his budget.
Reverting back to the salary question, why should it be determined that the Auditor General be of a rank of deputy minister, or is he supposed to be above the rank of deputy minister? Certainly now that he is going to be tied into the equivalent of a chief justice, he is taken out of the DM-1, the DM-3 or the DM-4 classifications. Is that because he is supposed to be independent of deputy ministers? Is that because he is to be paid like a judge rather than a deputy minister, although they are all at about the same level? Who decides what will be those relative salary levels?
I come back to a point that has been made by many members of this House. I do not know whether I have been the most vocal about it. It is absolute nonsense that we continue to have this arbitrary distinction or arbitrary setting of salaries on the part of government, which does not disclose for scrutiny the means or the reasons whereby salaries are set at that level. It seems to me that we have got to come around to another feature.
When we compare members of parliament with members of the judiciary, not so many years ago the salary of a member of parliament was the equivalent of that of a county court judge. He does not now receive half the salary of a county court judge. Do not include in there the MP's expense account, because the judge has an expense account which nobody takes into consideration. He receives $48,000 plus whatever may be the expenses of his office. No one says anything to him about that. I do not want to belabour the point, but it seems to me that we come around again to the question that there must be an independent advisory group, under statute, which every year or every second year revises or examines the salaries of the executive group of the public service, the judges, members of parliament, ministers of the Crown, and puts them all in relation. They do not have to be discussed here. They would come into force not on the initiative of the government unless a stated number, a goodly number of members of this House stood in opposition to the level of salaries proposed, or, shall we say, the executive level of government. At the moment there is a mishmash of illogicality, an unfairness. This particular point with regard to the Auditor General is a dead loss.
Now I come to the declaration of the President of the Treasury Board with regard to the new office of comptroller general. This person is to be designated as a deputy minister. Why? Is it for pecking order reasons? Is it for salary reasons? What is the salary going to be for the comptroller general? Is he going to be a DM-1, a DM-2 or a DM-3? What level? Surely to goodness, if there were a properly constituted advisory group whose recommendations have statutory effect, then these matters could be settled and it would not be at the whim of the government as to what level the remuneration would be set.
I will call it ten o'clock because I wish to make my last point tomorrow afternoon, Mr. Speaker.

April 25, 1977
Adjournment Debate
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-POSSIBILITY OF LEGISLATION TO EXTEND PRISONER OF WAR COMPENSATION TO VETERANS OF WORLD WAR I AND ESCAPERS AND EVADERS IN WORLD WAR II
VETERANS AFFAIRS-POSSIBILITY OF LEGISLATION TO EXTEND PRISONER OF WAR COMPENSATION TO VETERANS OF WORLD WAR I AND ESCAPERS AND EVADERS IN WORLD WAR II
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, March 25, as reported in Hansard at page 4340, I put this question to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald):
In view of the very real sympathy that the minister expressed in committee the other day for the 200 or so living veterans of World War I who were prisoners of war and also the interest he expressed in the Canadian veterans who were evaders or escapers in World War II, can he tell the House whether the chances are good that there will be legislation during this session to extend the prisoner of war compensation to these two groups of Canadian veterans?
The reply of the Minister of Veterans Affairs was to the effect that he was not in a position to make a commitment at that time but that the matter was under study in his department.
I then put to the minister a supplementary question in which I asked him whether study was also being given to the problem created by the fact that widows of veterans, where the veteran's disability pension was less than 48 per cent, are cut off without any pension on the death of the veteran. Again the minister assured me that this matter was under study by his department. Sir, what I have said adds up to three simple but direct questions that 1 should like to put to the minister. I thank him for being here at this hour of the night to respond to my questions. Many of us have made the case for each of these three groups of persons, so I do not feel that I need to make it again in tonight's brief session. I shall simply state each of the points.
It seems to me that there should be no further delay in granting the prisoner of war compensation which was provided last year for World Was II veterans to the 200 or so survivors of World War I. The cost would be infinitesimal compared with the moneys spent around this place, and it would be a declining cost. If we delay much longer, not many of the 200 will be left.
I also plead the validity of the case for escapers and evaders in World War II. A good deal has been written and said in recent months about their experiences during the war years, and it seemed to all of us who are members of the Standing Committee on Veterans Affairs that they, too, should receive the prisoner of war compensation which was provided by a bill we passed last year.
My third point has long been outstanding. It seems grossly unfair that if a veteran's pension was 48 per cent or more, and he dies, his widow gets the full widow's pension, which is 75

per cent of a full disability pension; but if a veteran's pension was below 48 per cent, when he dies his widow is cut off, with no pension at all. Many responsible bodies and groups have recommended that this should be corrected, that a pro rata pension should be paid in such cases. I dare to hope that some day we shall see that pro rata pension.
The three points I raise thus concern World War I veterans who were prisoners of war, World War II escapers and evaders who should get the same benefits as prisoners of war, and the revision of the pension rules regarding the widows of veterans where the veteran's pension was below 48 per cent. I hope the minister can update things for us tonight and indicate when we may expect legislation on those three important issues.

speakeroldname: Hon. Daniel J. MacDonald (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-POSSIBILITY OF LEGISLATION TO EXTEND PRISONER OF WAR COMPENSATION TO VETERANS OF WORLD WAR I AND ESCAPERS AND EVADERS IN WORLD WAR II
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I say what a pleasure it is to answer the questions raised by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). I shall deal with his questions, but in reverse order.
With respect to the suggested provision of pro rata pensions for widows of veterans where the veteran's pension was less than 48 per cent, let me say that the government is aware of all recommendations which have been made to provide pro rata pensions for widows of disability pensioners. At the present time a widow will be pensioned if her husband's death was attributable to service or was incurred during wartime. In addition, if her husband's pensionable disabilities were assessed at 48 per cent or more during his lifetime, the widow, as the hon. member said, would be eligible for widow's pension. This percentage was selected because at that rate the veterans were obviously seriously disabled and it was considered that the pensionable condition might play a part, however small, in the prisoner's death. On the other hand, if someone is pensioned at 5 per cent for flat feet and dies from a different cause, his death bears no relationship to his pensioned condition, and the question arises whether a pension should be paid for an unrelated death.
Canada does not take a back seat to any country in so far as our pension legislation is concerned. The benefits we provide for the disabled serviceman or woman, or their surviving dependants, are far greater than those provided by most other countries. I am not aware of any of our major western wartime allies who pay automatic survivor benefits to widows approaching the 48 per cent basis which we in Canada use.
Having said that, I must also say that the entire matter of veterans' benefits-and that includes pro-rata widow's pensions-is always under constant review by the Department of Veterans Affairs and by the Canadian Pension Commission and the other agencies of my ministry to see what changes can be made to improve the lot of the veterans and their dependants.
In the meantime, in the case of a veteran receiving even a 1 per cent disability pension, when he or she passes on, the surviving spouse and dependants can be supported on war veterans allowance. We do not feel that there is, or should be, any stigma attached to receiving WVA benefits. It is a right as
April 25, 1977

the legislation provides for it. Presently we have over 93,000 recipients of WVA benefits.
There is another matter which I would like to touch on briefly, and that is the possibility of legislation to extend prisoner of war compensation to veterans of World War I and escapees and evaders in World War II. I said recently, in answer to a question from the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, that I was not able to give any firm indication regarding this matter at this time.
As some hon. members are aware, representations have been made on behalf of both groups, and the matter is and will continue to be under active consideration.
Both subjects are deserving of careful study and I can assure the House that when progress has been made, I will report accordingly.

subtopic: POST OFFICE-PURPOSE OF INCREASE IN RATES-MEASURES TO RESTORE EFFICIENCY OF OPERATION
POST OFFICE-PURPOSE OF INCREASE IN RATES-MEASURES TO RESTORE EFFICIENCY OF OPERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 21 I directed a question to the Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) with respect to matters that I shall outline briefly this evening. I regret that the hon. gentleman is not with us- he was with us until a moment ago-because I think the matter I have to bring before the House would have provided him with an opportunity to give some specific replies that are not possible during the question period.
The first question deals with the rising cost of Post Office services, and was put in these terms:
Can the Postmaster General advise the House whether these regular increases are designed to decrease the Post Office deficit or to maintain the subsidy for an essential service?
The Postmaster General did not reply specifically and I think it was because he misunderstood the purport of my question. We are all concerned about the deteriorating state of Canada's postal service. It is one of the essential means of communication and I think it would have been an excellent opportunity for the Postmaster General to indicate if he regards this vital communications system as a service or as a business. Unfortunately he did not on that occasion, but I trust that whoever speaks for him tonight will indicate it because it is of vital importance and will decide whether or not we will overcome the continuing malaise in our postal service.
Incidentally, I was not necessarily speaking of the increase in the cost of stamps. Actually, in terms of the great distances in Canada it could be argued that perhaps mailing a first class letter is a bargain. What I was really thinking about was some of the more substantial increases, such as the price of postal boxes, the cancellation of the special registration fee as it applies to a special book rate, and so forth, increases that in some instances have gone up as much as 200 per cent or 300 per cent.
The second part of my question was of even greater importance. It was:
Adjournment Debate
... will the Postmaster General inform the House of the steps he has taken since taking over responsibility to restore Canada's Post Office to its former high efficiency?
Particularly I asked the Postmaster General what recommendations from the Hay's consultant report he had implemented. I asked that question because I had placed a question on the order paper asking for a tabling of this report. Unfortunately the tabling of the report was denied. I think that is also an unfortunate gesture on the part of the Postmaster General, because the only way we are going to come to any agreement on solutions is by open and honest discussion and dialogue, not by the consideration of private reports in secret in the offices of the bureaucracy of the Post Office Department.
I say this because in recent weeks I have had the opportunity to visit both Washington in the United States, and London, England, to see how they are dealing with their post office problems. All modern industrial countries have faced the same difficulties, and the solution adopted has been to proceed more or less rapidly toward mechanization and automation. In the United States postal system I discovered that they have come to grips with the problems which have been brought about by mechanization by having open discussion, mostly in congressional committees. Unfortunately we in the House of Commons have been denied that privilege. We do not have access to these reports which are put together at considerable cost to the taxpayers of Canada, and I think that is the only basis upon which we can make honest and fair appraisals of the situation.
The process is even more open in the United Kingdom. That is because they faced the impasse which confronts Canada, where at the moment labour unions are opposing mechanization. In 1972 the union of postal workers in the United Kingdom boycotted mechanization and refused to co-operate at all until they were allowed greater consultation in the process. As a result they have now been brought into the post office board. Their recommendations are listened to, and no major decision is made on mechanization and automation unless the union has had a chance to review it before the fact.
What has happened in Canada? The whole process has been put before the postal unions without any preliminary discussion or consultation. I was informed by both labour and management in the U.K. that some of the best and most useful ideas have come from the representatives of the postal union who sit on the post office board of directors. This is essentially what was behind my question.
1 regret that the Postmaster General did not reply in specific terms. I regret even more that he denied access to the Hays report, the most recent report, by refusing to table it. Incidentally, everyone has a copy of the report, but why should we have to work in secret? Why should the government have to work in secret? We are all anxious to work together to bring about a happier state of affairs in our Canadian post office. In the U.K. and in the U.S.A. the labour unions are strongly in support of mechanization and automation because they feel they are a vital part of the process. I think we could have the

April 25, 1977
Adjournment Debate
same positive reaction from our Canadian Union of Postal Workers if the same open policy of consultation were adopted in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Walter Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to Postmaster General):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Postmaster General
subtopic: POST OFFICE-PURPOSE OF INCREASE IN RATES-MEASURES TO RESTORE EFFICIENCY OF OPERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the questions posed by the hon. member on March 21 may well be on a single topic, restoration of efficiency within the Post Office Department, but I would like to provide a three-part answer, since the original question was so framed.
Are the regular postal increases designed to decrease the Post Office deficit or to maintain the subsidy for an essential service? In reply we can say that a perusal of the 1977-78 estimates shows that the deficit will be reduced slightly-yes, only to a small degree, but this should indicate the intention.
The second part of the hon. member's question related to steps taken by the present Postmaster General (Mr. Blais) to "restore Canada's Post Office to its former high efficiency." To this, we should emphasize that the major effort, the change in tactics, has been to move from confrontation to conversation. I have heard the hon. member say himself, within this House, that "perhaps the military posture of the Post Office is too deeply ingrained". "Consultation", he said, "which is important to human relations, is restricted to issuing an order".
We have introduced a new dimension-intergroup process. Intergroup development is a series of sessions which tend to begin as a confrontation. A third party is used as a moderator. This is designed to identify areas of difference and conflict between two parties. There is then, ideally, an agreement to solve problems jointly. The intergroup process calls for a candid exploration of conflicting points of view with a sincere belief that the two parties can arrive at a joint decision which is better than either could have arrived at individually.
Intergroup development is being tried where traditional labour/management relations methods have been tried and have failed. The Post Office's first intergroup session was begun with LCUC and management on a national level at Montebello last year. These meetings have continued into 1977. Another series of sessions was held near Moncton with regional, district, and local involvement. Now, much better understanding exists between LCUC and management. Further sessions will be established at regional, district, and local levels across the country.
In addition, we are holding preliminary discussions with regard to new contract demands. Our talks with the Letter Carriers' Union have proved encouraging. We have talked with two other unions and, if we cannot say things are as encouraging, at least it is a start.
Perhaps also we should mention that the Post Office has established ComTeam, a two-way employee-employer communications system that has, we believe, diffused some potentially explosive problems. In all, we are talking, we are not fighting, and that we believe is progress.
Finally, the hon. member asks what recommendations we have implemented from the Hays report. In reply to the hon.
[Mr. Dinsdale.J
member's request that we produce this report, motion No. 84, we stated that we would not since it is a confidential report intended for internal use. Following that answer, the hon. member realizes that we cannot comment on any aspect of that report. However, the hon. member knows that he can debate the refusal at a later time.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND- DATE OF SIGNING DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT-NATURE OF EXPENDITURES
REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND- DATE OF SIGNING DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT-NATURE OF EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on February 7 I raised with the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Lessard) the situation concerning the agreement in terms of expenditures in the next year or two in the Prince Edward Island comprehensive development plan. It was not until March 14 that the agreement on the expenditure of funds was concluded in Charlottetown, signed jointly by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion and the premier of Prince Edward Island.
On February 7 I asked the minister whether he could give us a date, which he did not know at that time, and perhaps more significantly whether he could indicate the exact details in terms of the priorities for the federal expenditures that will be made.
It was obvious at that time that some $30 million would likely be the rough figure of expenditure for this fiscal year, and that amount, and amounts almost equal to that over the next two years, as it turned out, will in fact be found in the agreement.
I am particularly concerned to find out from the minister what kind of efforts will be made in the area of public participation with respect to the increasing energy costs which are very much a factor in terms of the development of Prince Edward Island, the persistent problem of seasonal unemployment and, of course, the over-all framework of priorities that the federal government and this department will establish. While the minister was not able to inform me at that time as to the details, he did indicate in the latter part of his answer, after a supplementary, and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, I will try to provide the hon. member with as much detail as possible with regard to expenses and amounts which will be allocated to various sectors of the economic activity in the island, according to the agreement which has been signed. It is very detailed and I think the hon. member might be satisfied with it.
Certainly I hope to get that kind of detailed answer tonight. However, I am not overly optimistic. Frankly, since 1969 there has been a major decline, certainly a decline in terms of commitment to the concept of development, to putting Prince Edward Island more actively into the economic mainstream of Canada, and a serious decline as well in terms of lack of information. Whether the two go together, the decline in over-all commitment and the decline in information, remains to be seen, but I note from the press release issued on the day of the signing that there was virtually no information. In relation to this phase of the development plan it simply said:
April 25, 1977

The agreement signed today provides for a contribution by DREE of $89 million over the next three years for continuation of the phase two strategy. Programs implemented under this agreement are cost-shared on a 90-10 federal-provincial ratio except for school construction, which is 50-50. Emphasis will continue to be placed on the productive sectors: agriculture, fisheries and industrial development.
Interestingly enough, as part of the press coverage given to that signing event in Charlottetown, the Charlottetown Guardian carried the story:
Mr. Lessard indicated the general thrust would be toward job creation, stimulation of primary industry and establishment of small business.
However, the most significant and specific thing the minister said was reported as follows:
Monday's agreement specified that federal cost-sharing of some 300 provincial civil service jobs will be phased out over the next five years. It said the funding, which now amounts to about $5 million annually, will be terminated in roughly equal annual portions.
So it seems that the one specific aspect of this stage of the plan is not the creation of jobs but their reduction by some 300, and that the high-flown language concerning job creation and the stimulation of primary industry is merely window dressing to cover a substantial retreat on the part of the federal government.
The only other news in the local newspapers concerned a three-hour closed door discussion of funding and program proposals by federal and provincial officials. This was a meeting of the joint advisory board, a body well known to the islanders, at least. That three-hour closed door meeting tells more, I think, about the mentality and the psychology of the present approach to development by both the federal and provincial governments than anything I could say.
It seems to me that the joint advisory board is in effect the secret government of Prince Edward Island. This is the body which makes the priority decisions, decisions which are not the subject of public debate and which, very often, are not even announced. Often it is only well after the fact that islanders or Canadians generally learn that anything is going on with respect to the development plan.
I think it is incredible we should be subject to an approach of this kind with regard to developments which are so basic to our needs as the re-ordering of social and economic priorities. We are not told, for instance, about the relationship of priorities in various areas of expenditure to the growing amount of transfer payments in terms of equalization grants, unemployment insurance, old age assistance, or family allowances. We have no idea as to the relationship of priorities between departments in either the federal or the provincial governments and how they may be co-ordinated with the particular thrust of development in Prince Edward Island.
I think it is scandalous that the federal government, which is now committed to major developments in Prince Edward Island, should tell us so little in specific terms about its own priorities or the jointly agreed priorities of the two governments.
Adjournment Debate
This is not a program which started last month or last year. It was inaugurated in 1969, and agreement with respect to the second phase was signed in October, 1975. Yet islanders are increasingly in the dark as to the true nature and thrust of development, policies, and plans for Prince Edward Island. I hope we shall begin to reverse that process this evening and that the parliament secretary will tell us in specific terms the exact nature of the priorities which will be in effect in the next three funding years of the program, or that if he has insufficient time in which to do so this evening he will find an early opportunity of making all these details available.

subtopic: REGIONAL ECONOMIC EXPANSION-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND- DATE OF SIGNING DEVELOPMENT AGREEMENT-NATURE OF EXPENDITURES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to thank the hon. member for agreeing to postpone this debate until after the agreement had been signed.
On March 14 my minister met with Premier Campbell to sign an amendment to the Phase II Comprehensive Development Plan Agreement which provides funding arrangements for the next three years, amounting to $89 million: $30 million in the fiscal year 1977-78, $29,700,000 in 1978-79, and $29,300,000 in 1979-80.
On the same day the joint advisory board met to review the programs brought forward by plan management and to recommend allocation of funds. I would be pleased to provide the hon. member with the board's recommendations on the allocation of funds for the fiscal year 1977-78, as he requested.
However, Mr. Speaker, we would like it to be clearly understood that the development planning is a continuing process and must be capable of responding to opportunities as they arise; programs are instruments of long range objectives and as such are subject to change. It is only possible therefore to provide precise accounting after the fiscal year has ended.
I am also able to provide a detailed account of federal expenditures, in Phase II, for 1975-76. A similar accounting for 1976-77 will be available in a few months.
We believe that if programs and funds are secured too firmly to an inflexible system, many worthy projects could be lost or weakened by delay. For example, in February a project to increase and stabilize the income of Prince Edward Island lobster fishermen was introduced under the development plan although six months earlier it had not been anticipated in the year's budget. The project was designed by both governments and the Prince Edward Island Fishermen's Association in response to a specific need, and should begin to show results this coming lobster season.
In summary then, Mr. Speaker, we have a budget proposal for 1977-78, and a detailed accounting for 1975-76. I am prepared to provide the hon. member with detailed data for subsequent fiscal years as it becomes available.
Further, I am sure the hon. member will be in attendance next week at the committee meetings. We have set aside three days for the Atlantic region. I think he has some very specific questions that he would like to ask, and the minister will be available to answer them in more detail than can be provided here in three minutes.
Motion agreed to and the House adjourned at 10.28 p.m.
